speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter to which I beg to call the attention of the government, and particularly the attention of the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding). It is in reference to the bounties on iron and steel as contained in the statutes of 1896, 1897 and 1899. The Bounty Act of 1897 provides for a bounty on steel ingots, puddled iron bars, and pig iron manufactured in Canada, specifying the amounts per ton which the producers of steel may be entitled to. That Act was amended in 1S99, and the statute sets out, with considerable detail, the extent of the bounty which may be earned by those producing iron and manufacturing steel in the Dominion of Canada. A few days ago the press of the country contained the prospectus of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, of Sydney, Cape Breton, over the signature of Mr. Moxham, the general manager of that vast industry, and among the attractions specified in that prospectus I find the following ;

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.

speechtext:
If the production from the company's works be as estimated, 300,000 tons of pig metal and 60.000 tons of steel blooms in 1901, and thereafter 400,000 tons of iron and steel per annum, made from foreign (Newfoundland) ore, the bounties to be received from the Canadian government will be as follows ;-
1901		 $ 870,000
1902		 2,075,000
1903		 1,850,000
1904		 1,450,000
1905		 1,000,000
1906		 625,000
1907		 225,000

In tlie seven years the bounties to be paid by the government of Canada to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company would amount in the aggregate to $8,095,000. It may not be fair for me to surmise, that taking into consideration the vast resources at the disposal of this company, and the tremendous increase in the iron trade probable in the next few years, that that bounty is likely to be double the amount indicated here. Now, Mr. Speaker, if we were confined to paying bounties even to this one company, in my opinion, the matter would be sufficiently serious, but I find that the Cramp Ontario Steel Company have also issued a prospectus, in which they give us an idea of their expectations with respect to this great industry.
They also are in a position to earn and will earn a very large bounty. Then there are other large industries In the Dominion, all of which come under this Act. What I wish to draw the attention of the government to is this, that the Dominion of Canada stands to pay out a very large amount of money in the way of bounties, and I would like to know whether it is too late for the government to take such steps as may, While not invading any vested rights, at the same time prevent further vested interests growing up under the Act. There is no doubt that the principle of granting bounties to industries under certain conditions is a proper one, and one which has been adopted by governments in all civilized countries in the world ; but at the same time it strikes me that in these cases there may be an invasion of that principle. For instance, we find by the prospectus of the Dominion Iron and Steel Co. that they have a capital of some $23,000,000, and they have on their directorate some of the leading financial people of Canada, the United States and Great Britain-men of whom in no sense can it be said that they are financially in dire need of any assistance in respect to any industry or concern to which they may attach themselves. At this juncture-and it is not too early-I think the government should take into their serious consideration this question of the bounty on iron and steel. It may be that the volume of business generated, and the amount of money expended in and about these industries may be commensurate with the amount of bounty the people of this Dominion are obliged to pay to these companies. It is not my intention, in directing the attention of the government to this matter, to advocate the invasion of any vested right that may have been established by this Act. Doubtless the Act was passed with a view to helping the struggling industries of this country ; but I do not think anybody would characterize the Dominion Iron and Steel Co. or the Ontario Cramp Steel Co. as struggling industries that would require such a large amount of tiie money of the taxpayers of Canada
to be given to them in order to earn their dividends.
I would like very much if the government would give us some assurance that the proper interests of the people will be safeguarded in this respect. I think it is a matter of very great importance, and one that interests every taxpayer in the Dominion. The amount of money which will be paid in bounties must be very large ; in the seven years it might amount to anywhere from $25,000,000 to $50,000,000. I am not an alarmist, but taking the statements of these companies themselves, and the tremendous output which is likely to attend the successful operation of their works, there is every indication that the amount of the bounty will at any rate exceed $15,000,000 within the seven years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should not care to give a definite answer to the statement which forms the main point of my hon. friend's question, that is to say, whether or not parliament might properly place any restrictions upon the amount which would become payable under these bounty Acts. The matter has already received some consideration, and 1 am not disposed to give any answer to-day which would tie the hands of the government as to their future course. Of course, there is one thing we must clearly understand, that though how far there may be vested rights is a debatable question, yet in so far as we may agree that there are any vested rights arising under these Acts, those vested rights must he respected. There have been on the statute-books of Canada for many years Acts respecting bounties on iron and steel, and in those Acts there has never been any limitation as to the quantity on which a bounty would be paid. In fact, I think the great difficulty hitherto has been that the Acts were not effective in producing a large development of the iron and steel iudustry. I am afraid that the inference might almost be drawn from my hon. friend's remarks, although he might object to it, that if this industry had jogged along in the old way and only made small demands on the treasury, it would be all right ; but inasmuch as is has got out of the old rut and has developed on a large scale, it is all wrong. I should not like to accept that conclusion. I think, perhaps, there is a tendency on the part of the promoter of a company, when issuing his prospectus, to put his best foot forward ; and if he has any government advantages, he is not likely to underestimate them. Therefore, I should not be very much alarmed at the statements of a very rose-coloured character made in the prospectus of any company organized under this bounty system. Still, it is well to point out that the only matter of difference between us on the two sides of the House as respects this Bounty Act was that while we were will-

ing to pay $2 a ton to this Cape Breton corporation on the iron it might produce, my hon. friend who was at that time the leader of the opposition, was quite willing to pay $3 a ton, because he thought we should treat the iron ore of the colony of Newfoundland just the same as we treat the iron ore of the Dominion itself. On that view there would be paid on all the iron produced in Cape Breton from Newfoundland ore the full bounty, whereas in reality we shall properly treat it as a foreign ore entitled to receive only the minimum bounty. I do not, however, feel very much alarmed over the matter, even if we should be called upon to pay a very large sum under this system. We may perhaps agree that if the industry was worth encouraging at all, it was worth being made successful, and on a large scale. One thing is certain, iron and steel cannot be produced in such enormous quantities, either in Cape Breton or in other parts of the Dominion, without there being an enormous development of the business of the country, from which the Dominion in one form or other will receive a very large return. There is that comfort to us in the first place. There is the further comfort that even if this system should result in the payment of large sums of money, that payment will speedily come to an end, because at the very time we provided the scale of bounties, we stated that it was regarded by us as of vital importance that the bounties should be gradually reduced by the terms of the Act itself ; so that after a term of five years, beginning on the 1st of July next, the bounties will cease to exist. If, therefore, for a short time we should be called upon to pay even a large sum for the development of these industries, we would have the comfort of knowing in the meantime that as a result of that experiment there must grow up a vast amount of business in the Dominion which would not probably have grown up except for that development; and that if the bounty should be large, it can only continue for five years, when it will be wiped off the statute-book. And if at the end of that period we should find ourselves with a tremendous development of the iron and steel industry-and my hon. friend knows that it will be not only in Cape Breton, but also in the province of Ontario, where great works are projected-and if that result should be achieved at considerable cost to the public treasury, I am not sure that we would regret it; for we would have established throughout the Dominion great industries which would undoubtedly have a tremendous effect in developing the prosperity of the whole 'country.

PRIOR (Victoria, B.C.) When the hon. member for Westminster rose to draw attention to the bounty system, I was in hopes, ill'. Speaker, that instead of finding fault, he was going to urge the necessity I Mr. FIELDING.
for an extension of that system, especially in the province of British Columbia. The hon. gentleman is an old resident of that province, and knows its immense resources. He knows that the people of British Columbia look forward to a not far distant day when we shall have iron works started there ourselves, and he must know that it is impossible to get such works started without a bounty. I do not understand why he should have so much anxiety concerning the large amount Canada may have to pay. As the hon. Finance Minister has pointed out, whenever an amount is paid for bounty, there is considerably more added to the wealth of Canada, as on every ton of iron manufactured a large sum of money is paid out in wages and material. I have in my hand a newspaper clipping, giving a report of the convention of the Boards of Trade of British Columbia held at Greenwood. One of the resolutions passed is the following :
Whereas, there is at present no lead refining, works in the Dominion of Canada, and the initial cost of establishing such a plant is very great, it is the opinion of this association that the Dominion government should encourage the establishment of such a plant by a grant for a term of years of a bounty of $5 per ton upon ail lead of Canadian origin smelted and refined in Canada.
That is one of the resolutions passed by the associated boards of trade at its annual convention, and it shows the feelings of the business men of that province. With that resolution X am heartily in accord, and I am sorry to see an hon. gentleman get up and endeavour to lead this House to believe that the people he represents are not in favour of the bounty system, but are in favour of its being carefully watched at least, if not entirely done away with. Let me say that even if millions be expended in bounties, we would get an ample return for our expenditure from the work done in the smelters. In British Columbia, the business interests are not only asking for a bounty on lead refining, but are looking forward to government assistance to the ship building industry in Vancouver and Victoria. In fact, we hope soon to see the day when the Pacific coast will be the great manufacturing section of the Dominion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
This sum of money is asked to continue the work which has been going on for several years-for many years I might say -in the St. Lawrence. The depth of the water in the St. Lawrence between Quebec and Montreal was supposed to be 27* feet. But. in 1895, and also in 1897, the water fell. In 1895, during three days of the month of November, the water fell so low that the depth was only 25 feet 10 inches. It was then found necessary to adopt a new basis. When I took office, I may say, the department was not equipped. In 1888 the late government had taken from the harbour commissioners both the work on the channel and their equipment-their plant. Before I took office, my predecessor had built one new dredge, the Laval. Since then, we have built the Laurier, the Lady Aberdeen, and the Lady Minto, and we have another dredge in course of construction, which will be completed by the
first of June. Of these four dredges, two are steel dredges. Perhaps I may be permitted to say, to the honour of our Canadian workingmen, that these four dredges last built, are, as I claim, the best dredges of their kind in America. That may be saying a good deal, but I am quite sure that I am correct in making that statement. We are now dredging the channel to a width of 450 feet, and a depth practically of 30 feet. During the last season, which is practically the first during which the work was carried on, we dredged to the depth of 30 feet, a distance of a little more than ten miles. The intention of the department is to dredge to the width and depth I have named the whole channel, so that about fifty miles remains to be dredged. Within the last fortnight, I have signed a contract with the Poison Iron Works for the construction of a suction dredge, which will have a capacity of between 30,000 and 40,000 yards a day. It seems almost incredible that a dredge could do such a quantity of work. I have seen one of these dredges myself ; in fact, the decision to build this dredge is the result of a trip I made with the deputy minister_ to New York to inspect machines of this kind. We expect to be able to complete the work of deepening and widening the channel within the next season. It may be that we shall be deceived by a few months ; but, if there is no accident, I fully anticipate that the whole work of deepening and widening the St. Lawrence in the way I have just pointed out, will be completed in the next season.

speechtext: I think I have that information here. I would not bind myself to exact figures, but I am told by the chief engineer that the quantity in Lake St. Peter alone is 90,000,000 cubic yards.

speechtext: What is the capacity of the dredges now working ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The capacity of the best dredges that are now working-and working night and day- would vary between 7,000 and 8,000 cubic yards a day. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) knows very well that the capacity of a dredge depends a good deal upon the material in which it works. If you strike a boulder or a difficult spot the dredge,

powerful as it may be, cannot do the same amount of work as In soft material. In Lake St. Peter the work is in soft material, and we expect to do that work with the new suction dredge, which is to be completed by the middle of August. I may say in passing that four of the dredges that I have at work now are equipped with electric light so that they are capable of working during the night as well as by day. We intend to equip with electric light the new dredges that are now being built.
Several questions have been raised as to the work now going on. Of course, the main object of deepening and widening the St. Lawrence is to enable the largest ships to come up to Montreal. The Montreal business men have no ambition to monopolize the trade of this country, but Montreal is so located that unless the trade from the west is brought down there, it is certain, I am very much afraid, to go to American ports. Two and two make four, and cannot make five. Now, between the port of Buffalo and the Port of New York the distance by rail is 445 miles. The New York Central have made their road between these two points just as level as the floor of this Chamber. So fine is that road that they are able to attach between 75 and 100 cars to a single locomotive, and draw that immense load to their terminus in the city of New York.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What has that got to do with our canals ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I will try to show you what it has got to do. Now, the grain comes, as we all know, from the American and Canadian west to Canadian ports. Trade has no law, it goes where it pays best. From Port Colborne to Montreal by water is 375 miles. When the works at Port Colborne are completed we will have a harbour there, which we have not to-day. It is almost incredible that we have no harbour there yet, and how can we expect to have trade ? There is Buffalo on [DOT]one side, with a magnificent harbour, with a breakwater, with about sixty elevators, a port fully equipped, giving a depth of 22 feet; while on our side we have no harbour accommodation whatever. How can trade flowr through our Welland canal to Montreal when big ships cannot load and unload, when big ships cannot enter at Port Colborne to-day ? It is out of the question for shipping to anchor there, the harbour is solid rock. The works at Port Colborne will be completed for the accommodation of trade within a short time, my department has awarded a contract for the erection of a breakwater, and the Minister of Railways and Canals is going on with the works for the canal itself ; and when we have proper accommodation there, the big carriers of grain that now go to Buffalo, and must go there because they cannot go anywhere else, will then be able to come to our Canadian

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
ports to load and unload, and transhipment will take place at Port Colborne.
Whether we have 14 feet of water-I have every reason to believe that we have 14 feet-but whether we have that or only 13 feet, or 131 feet, we are certainly in a better position than our American friends with their Erie canal. Then, our Canadian system of canals, with its terminal at Montreal, will be a competitor with the American railways. I do not take the Erie canal into account at all. To-day it is little more than a small ditch, if I may say so without offence it is out of date, and cannot in any respect compete with the great system of American railways, nor with the great system of Canadian canals. On the one hand we have Port Colborne and the Welland canal, 375 miles from Montreal.
On the other hand we have the Parry Sound Railway. The government has, so far, not done much to help the enterprising gentleman who has completed, at his own expense and at his own risk, the Parry Sound Railway. I have asked for tenders for the erection of a breakwater which will enable Mr. Booth, or anybody else, to erect elevators if they wish. When that elevator is completed and when Mr. Booth has completed his work, Parry Sound will be a first-class port. During the past season the Parry Sound Railway has been the principal carrier of grain to Montreal, by the aid of the St. Lawrence route. Unfortunately, that rail-way system has not yet reached the city of Montreal independently. To-day Mr. Booth is obliged to tranship his grain at Coteau Landing and take it in barges to the port of Montreal. In spite of that difficulty, Mr. Booth has been able to carry grain at a profit to the city of Montreal, though not a large profit. Why is he able to do this ? Because he is able to get the western trade. Not many people believed, two or three years ago, that the Parry Sound Railway would be a competitor with the American railways in getting a return trade, but it has done so. You would be surprised to learn, Mr. Chairman, the amount of return trade that Mr. Booth has been able to capture between New Tork and Chicago. And so the Parry Sound system is another feeder to the port of Montreal and to the St. Lawrence route.
A good deal has been said lately of the project of improving the French river. I have read speeches-I have no right, I suppose, to refer to them here-referring to that scheme. I wish the House would give its close attention to that project. The question whether the Canadian Pacific Railway will carry the trade going to North Bay will not prevent anybody from giving that scheme his favourable consideration. From the mouth of the French river on the Georgian Bay to North Bay is 50 miles.
I make bold to say that with the expenditure of about $2,000,000-1 cannot bind myself to any figure, of course, but I have rea-

son to believe that with an expenditure of $2,000,000, that waterway between North Bay by the French river to Georgian Bay, can be made 20 feet deep.

speechtext: I have not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Have you any idea as to the quantity ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The only trade point I investigated was as to the grain trade.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: That freight is coming east.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes. I will be very glad indeed to bring down that information.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: When the minister was speaking, I understood him to refer to the gratifying fact that the Booth road was able to obtain a quantity of the traffic moving westward toward Chicago. If the hon. minister could tell us the tonnage of that traffic it would be very interesting information.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I had the pleasure of a conversation with Mr. Booth a few days ago, and he told me that he had handled a very large amount of return freight, and that if he had been able to get accommodation he would have been in a position to make contracts for double the quantity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Accommodation where ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: He did not tell me how much it was, but I will be glad to ask him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Where was the accommodation lacking ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Of course he lacks accommodation in Montreal, and he wants more accommodation at

Parry Sound. Mr. Booth has built a large elevator at the latter place, and I suppose he has spent nearly a million dollars of his money there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What is the cost per yard of this excavation at Montreal ? When you dredge it out, do the prisms remain perfect or does it require a dredge all the time to keep it open.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We have only a couple of places, and these not important, at which we are obliged to dredge occasionally. Lake St. Peter was dredged fifteen years ago, and it will be a pleasure for the House to know that the middle of the channel is deeper to-day than it was then. The St. Lawrence does not fill in. We had a little accident a couple of years ago at one point, where there had been some little filling in of sand, but not of much importance. As to the cost of dredging it varies, but I think I may say that the suction dredge we have contracted for will be able to dredge at about half a cent a yard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Half a cent a yard ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Oh, yes. The cost of dredging with our last improved dredges varies from 3 cents, 5 cents, 6 cents, to 7 cents. Of course some of the dredges cost more, for when you strike a boulder it may take a day to get it out, but with our improved dredges the cost has been reduced very greatly indeed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: This information confirms the statements I made last year in the House as to the cost of dredging. I drew the attention of the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) to the cost of dredging at Liverpool and New York, and today the Minister of Public Works tells us that he can do dredging in the St. Lawrence at a less rate than 1 cent per cubic yard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: In soft material.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Oh. yes, I understand that. I congratuate the minister on getting the improved style of suction dredge which has been adopted in European countries and in the United States, and it is the dredge above all others that we ought to have had long ago in the St. Lawrence. Y'ou have no harbour accommodation at Montreal suitable for the western trade, even if you do open up the St. Lawrence route. I understand from Mr. Booth and others interested in the trade, that the amount of grain deposited in Montreal is limited to the accommodation. I had hoped from the statement of the minister, made some three or four years ago, when his plan for better accommodation at Montreal was adopted, that the work would be carried out by this time, and I am sorry to say that because of force of circumstances,
or deficiency in the treasury, or through being overpowered by his colleagues in the government, he has been unable to carry out what he promised. The minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte), has given us his obiter dicta without tlie authority of the rest of his colleagues, as to his intentions with regard to deepening the French river from the Georgian Bay to Lake Nipissing, and I congratulate him on entertaining this idea. Not only would it accommodate the trade of the west, but it will open up facilities for the Canadian Pacific Railway. Of course we must not say anything about that because if it favours a railway some people say it is an incubus on the country, but we all know that anything by which the trade of that railway will be developed at the port of Montreal will be for the benefit of the community at large. There is another point to which I wish to refer briefly. I believe that the building of the Georgian Bay canal will be in the interest of Montreal, and in the interest of all Canada, and that canal must be built in the future. The minister speaks about a twenty foot navigation, which is the navigation of Lake Superior and the upper lakes, and there is no necessity for having more than that on the mitre sills of the locks. But, let there be plenty of breadth and plenty of length in the locks, and then steamers of almost any burden can proceed to Montreal, because with twenty feet in depth you can build steamers broad enough and long enough to carry seven or eight thousand tons. These steamers could carry coal from the maritime provinces to the upper lakes and return with cargoes of grain. I predict that some day the Georgian Bay canal will be built. I agree with the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that if not a single boat passed down the St. Lawrence canals, and if we got no direct benefit from them, yet the people of this country would receive a return for the seventy-five million dollars expended on the canals by the very fact of their being there and the influence they have in reducing freight rates generally. I trust the minister will be able to make a harbour at Port Colborne. His present proposition does not contemplate a harbour, but rather the construction of a couple of piers for the purpose of constructing elevators. If you try to make that a harbour I am afraid you will have to make an expenditure largely in excess of the amount that has been stated, for I believe it will cost three or four million dollars. And what benefit is it to the country ? It is to enable vessels of twenty-two feet draft to tranship at Port Colborne for the purpose of their freight being taken down the River St. Lawrence.
If they went fifteen miles further they could go to the port of Buffalo, tranship there, and come down the St. Lawrence as well as from Port Colborne. You will never make a port at Port Colborne that will at all

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I did not state that that was on a cargo going from Montreal. I stated that it was on vessels leaving a point on the St. Lawrence further down- a place called Bic. I stated that on four ships going down the river 14 and 15 guineas per cent insurance had been asked, and by taking no risk we got it done for 10 shillings. That was in November.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
It is very gratifying to find that on questions affecting our national security, men of both political parties generally agree. This

question of the St. Lawrence route is above party politics, and I will always be only too glad to receive suggestions from my bon. friends opposite, as well as my friends on this side. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is quite right in urging me to have the port of Montreal properly equipped. I admit that it is not equipped as it should have been long ago. But this country is large, the requirements of Canada have exacted from us the expenditure of vast sums of money, and we have not been able to do everything at once. Now, however, the hour has come when this question must be solved. The harbour commissioners are carrying out very great improvements in the port of Montreal. Large docks and basins are being erected. One of the docks is completed, another will be finished in a few months, and the third in a year or so. These are high level wharfs, upon which permanent structures can be erected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We want something more.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I know that these works are only the beginning. The government is building a wharf in the eastern portion of the city- that unfortunate eastern portion, against which so much has been said, but which should have been equipped long ago. I know that we have not the requisite facilities. Any one who has travelled over the world with his two eyes open knows that we are nowhere in the port of Montreal, but there are so many people who have not travelled as much as they should, and I am very much afraid that some of our Montreal friends belong to that class. I am happy to say, however, that there is a great improvement in this respect in that city. The young generation is asserting itself, and my hon. friends will agree with me that the ships now coming to that port have improved in size, capacity and in carrying power, but we must have something more.
The insurance question has been dealt with by my hon. friend in a way upon which I could not improve. The Lloyds, 1 am sorry to say, have taken us by the throat. When they say that they have incurred terrible losses, they always forget to give us the number of years during which these losses have occurred. Ten or fifteen years ago the St. Lawrence route was much more dangerous than it is to-day, and this remark may be applied to the statement made to the House a day or two ago by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence, Montreal (Mr. Bickerdike). I asked him how many years the losses he gave covered, and he answered me that they covered a period of eleven years. I make' bold to say that during the last three or four years there were fewer accidents in the St. Lawrence than ever before. In point of fact, 38
the St. Lawrence is in a better condition than it has ever been. I have had built testing scows and implements, and twice a year the whole length of the St. Lawrence is swept and tested, so that the shipping community may be completely assured that there are no obstacles in the channel. Nearly the whole channel has been scraped, and the curves have been straightened and obstacles removed, and during the last four years we have done most useful and profitable work.
I must take exception to what my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has said about the work at Port Colborne. I hope that he is mistaken in his view. I have given a good deal of attention to that port. I have been there myself several times to try and understand the position better. I have asked for tenders for a breakwater from the Point on a length of 5,700 feet, and have received a tender from Hogan & McDonald, for the sum of $395,000. When that breakwater is built, any vessel drawing 20 feet of water will be able to take shelter behind it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Are they building the breakwater and deepening the harbour besides ?	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Yes, they deepen a part of the harbour so that they may use the dredged material to fill the cribwork. The area to be dredged first will be small, but I may say without hesitation, that with a pretty small sum !t would be possible to have sufficient area to give shelter to ships. When that breakwater is built, and when the works going on under the direction of the Minister of Railways and Canals are completed, the largest carriers on the lakes will be able to load and unload in that port. Would it be sufficient, from a national standpoint, to rely on the port of Buffalo ? Is it not clearly better that the ships carrying the trade of the St. Lawrence route should go to a Canadian port and unload there ? My hon. friend is afraid that we will be obliged to incur a large expenditure. But if, with a moderate sum, we can make ourselves independent, that will be a great deal better for us than relying on the port of Buffalo. In all these commercial and national questions, our motto should be ' Canada first.' We must be independent of anybody, we must make ourselves at home in Montreal, on the lakes and in our winter ports. We should give the best possible attention to these matters, and make Canada an independent nation from a commercial standpoint. You do not know what may happen tomorrow. You do not know what Congress may decide to-morrow. Why. a few weeks ago, the Bo^rd of Trade of New York wanted to boycott Montreal and even Portland. and I suspect that the last move of the Grand Trunk Railway in settling itself in Portland was. to a large extent, dictated by American influence. Well, Sir, I say it is



our duty, tlie duty of both sides of the House, to make this country at home in *these large national questions.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I had not intended to say anything at all in this matter, but as the hon. minister has invited an expression of opinion by members on both sides, I shall say a few words. While I do not wish to find fault with the spending of money in deepening Port Colborne harbour-for I think it is necessary that the harbour should be iu such a shape as to be lit to receive large vessels with a deep draught-yet, I do think that what money is spent on Port Colborne harbour should be spent with a view to having, later on, a Welland canal large enough to receive the largest class of vessels. The navigation of the great lakes is a different style of navigation from that of the River St. Lawrence. The River St. Lawrence from Kingston, or, if you prefer it, from Prescott, down, is practically a canal, that is, it is a canal with stretches of river which are the same as canals in not calling for such a staunch style of vessels as are necessary on the lakes. Practically the great lakes are small seas, and the style of craft necessary there is one that would be practically safe upon the ocean itself. From Duluth, or from Chicago, to the beginning of the St. Lawrence proper, that is, to the foot of Lake Ontario, is a chain of lake navigation. That is broken at the Welland canal now. The hon. minister should not lay out his work with the intention of having what we may call the small Welland canal-that is, a canal of a size which will accommodate the present modern size of boat. I desire to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that from Port Colborne to Kingston and from Port Dalhousie to Kingston, the navigation calls for the same style of vessel, so far as seaworthiness and style of navigation are concerned, so far as the class of officer and seamen are concerned, as is required on the upper lakes. Therefore, it is not wise for the hon. minister to proceed as though the Welland canal were to be made part of a chain of river navigation, because after the Welland canal is passed and Lake Ontario is entered, there is a stretch of lake navigation before the river navigation begins. As I sny, tbe navigation of the river does not call for so staunch a style of vessel or so expensive a crew. Take, for instance, the present style of craft now navigating the St. Lawrence-with a capacity of 25,000 or 30,000 bushels and costing $8,000 or $9,000 when new, pin flats, as they are called, which carry most cheaply. Of course, if you can carry your grain iu a craft that does not cost more than thirty or forty cents a bushel to build, you have an advantage over a style of vessel that costs twice as much, such vessels as are necessary for the navigation of the lakes. The point I seek to make is that there are Mr. TARTE.
two great chains of navigation, the lake chain to the foot of Lake Ontario, and then the river chain from the foot of Lake Ontario to Montreal. The object of tbe government should he to make each chain complete. As the hon. minister has asked for suggestions, I would suggest also that the tolls might be taken off the Welland canal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What are the tolls ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: They amounted last year to something over $100,00O, which Is a small amount of money compared with the interest on the expenditure represented in the canal. These tolls are a direct hindrance to trade. Take the tolls on coal, for example. The toll-rate on coal on the Welland canal is twenty cents a ton. Why, coal has been carried from Buffalo to Chicago or Buffalo to Duluth, for 25 cents a ton ; so you can see what a barrier this toll of 10 cents a ton must be, and bow it will restrict the carrying of merchandise through our canal system. The result has been that tbe carriage of coal through the Welland canal has been cut down to about half to what it was two or three years ago. So far as canals are concerned, we meet the Americans at two points, once at the Soo, where both our canal and the American canal are free, and again at Port Colborne, where we have a canal with tolls, while the Americans have a canal on which no tolls are charged. Our trade is handicapped to that extent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I only wish to say a very little on this subject. It seems to me that the question resolves itself into two points, and what I regard as the important things in giving us control of the transportation of our own country are something like the following : First, we should make the channel between Montreal and Quebec what it ought to he as regards depth, and we should have it well lighted. The hon. minister is directing his attention towards that end at the present time, and I feel satisfied that both sides of the House will support him in that policy. Any reasonable expenditure looking towards that end will be in the right direction, and will he in the interests of Canadian shipping and of Canada. Following that, it seems to me, means should be devised to reduce the cost of insurance. For that is the next large item interfering with the trade by the St. Lawrence. It appears to me, from what has been written of late on tbe subject, that the government might well join some insurance company in sharing the risk or guaranteeing a portion of the risk for some years to come, at least until a business is built up by an insurance company, and we can be independent of outside insurance companies. In the meantime, to ascertain what risks are incurred, we ought to have better data than we have with regard to the losses that have

taken place (luring the last few years on that route. Surely we have the facts somewhere in connection with our returns of shipping or of trade and navigation in this country. We ought to have these facts and so be able to estimate what it would cost to insure trade by this route, and then join some company, or else the government become the insurers themselves. It must seem to most people that the insurance paid *on this route at the present time is out of all proportion to the dangers incurred in carrying on the shipping by the St. Lawrence route. Then, I think, improvement ought to go on in the harbour of Montreal, because, it seems evident, from what the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) tells us, it is very much out of date. The hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is causing expenditure to be made with the object of improving our equipment in this respect. Whether that expenditure is as rapid as it ought to be or not, I am not prepared to say ; but at least, I think, we ought to exercise greater enterprise in trying to bring it to a successful conclusion than we are doing at the present time. We should have improved means of handling freight; the time spent by vessels in coming in and going out, in loading and unloading, should be made as short as possible. These matters might well engage the attention of the minister, because the inconveniences that now exist may be the means of driving vessels that hitherto have sought the St. Lawrence route to go to Boston or other ports for their trade. These improvements seem to be of the greatest need at the present time, and I think co-ordinate with them we might well improve the waterways above Montreal, leading to that port. The minister says he is directing his energies towards that end at the present time. and I think he is entitled to credit so far as he is doing so upon intelligent lines. But I must confess that I have felt for some time past that the proposed expenditure, especially at Port Colborne, is not likely to bring the return which the minister expects or desires, and that perhaps the same amount of money might be spent in other directions that would bring a better return. The ex-Minister of Railways stated that when Buffalo affords facilities for vessels going fifteen miles further and transhipping, it is very doubtful whether the improvements the minister is making at Port Colborne are likely to be a sufficient inducement to make vessels go there and unload instead of going to Buffalo, if they desire to tranship there and go on down to the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Port Colborne and the Canadian system of canals will be competitors of the Buffalo route. If we were to place ourselves in the hands of our opponents, how could we fight against them ?
38}

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I admit there is a serious obstacle to be overcome, and one which is worthy of consideration. We practically handicap ourselves to a certain extent for that trade. If we could provide facilities for transhipment at Port Colborne by way of docks, elevators and depth of water, no doubt we would be acting largely in the right direction ; but whether that would accomplish the end we have in view must be for the future to determine. But I say that our own waterways might be improved very well at the same time.
Now, there seems to be a serious contention between people in this country as to whether we have or have not fourteen feat of water above Montreal. Many shippers say we have not. I believe some are afraid to risk a trial. Others say we have. I see that the Montreal Witness says that we have not, and I presume they would scarcely write a hap-hazard without some definite knowledge on that subject. They contended last year that we had not. It is claimed by others we have such a depth. But if we have not, the sooner we have the better, and the more urgently we should direct oar endeavours towards securing that end in the interest of shipping.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What would the hon. gentleman suggest ought to be done that has not been done in order to assure owners of vessels of the existence of this fourteen foot channel ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I think there ought to be soundings along the whole channel where there is supposed to be a less depth.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Does not the hon. gentleman know that there is no portion of the channel that has not been sounded, no portion that has not been swept from one entrance to the other with the most improved appliances for that purpose ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I may add that in some respects rivers are under the care of the Public Works Department, and I made up my mind last year to understand the whole question, and for that purpose I ordered a survey to be made. At this moment a survey is going on between Kingston and Prescott. A survey will be completed in the course of next year, not only of the channel but of the whole river ; so we will be perfectly sure of the depth, not only of the channel but of the whole volume of the river. So far as I am concerned, I have consulted with many shippers in Montreal, and they are all convinced that we have a fourteen foot channel. The Minister of Railways and Canals stated that clearly the other evening. What other means we could take, I do not see.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman has given us information himself of what they are doing, and he is doing just what I was going to suggest, that is, making soundings and then publishing charts of the soundings, so as to settle the question to the satisfaction of those who are interested in navigation. I am not contending that we have not that depth, but so long as there is uncertainty in the public mind it deters shippers from running the risk. Now, when that is done, I trust the Minister of Public Works will direct his attention towards improving the upper lake harbours. I am glad to say that he is doing it. I have no fault to find, nor do I wish to be understood as finding fault with what he has done, because I am only suggesting what should be done in this connection. But after all, it is claimed by some that we cannot get trade through our ports and down our canals. I may mention here that we are sometimes at a loss on this side of the House whether to look to the Minister of Railways and Canals or to the Minister of Public Works, because sometimes it seems that the Minister of Public Works is usurping the functions of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and vice versa. But so long as they are working in the same direction, it is all right.
But after that is all done, it seems to me that we might go further and do something more to induce shipping to come through our own channels and down to our own ports. Looking up the history of shipping in other countries some years ago-1 am speaking with an indistinct recollection, and may not be accurate-I found that some countries have determined to give a bounty on shipping going through their own ports and down their own channels. It seems to me we might do something in that direction. We have our own ports and our own lake vessels. It seems to me we might give a bounty upon all vessels that will carry produce, say from the port of Montreal instead of from the port of Boston, or that will carry produce from the port of Halifax, or the port of St. John, or the port of Quebec, instead of from American ports. We might give all shippers landing goods at those ports some rebate upon their cargoes, so that - vessel-owners might get some consideration for landing in our ports. It is not necessary to make it a large one, but frequently a small bounty would be a sufficient inducement to make vessel-owners land their cargoes in a Canadian port. I think this point is worthy of consideration on the part of the government. Let them look into the question carefully, and see if something could not be done in that direction. We might give a consideration to the vessels of our own country larger than we would give to the vessels belonging to a foreign country ; but give some consideration to foreign vessels as well, if they will land cargoes in our own ports and take Mr. TARTE.
cargoes from our own ports to foreign countries. Let us give a consideration to the trade that is carried through our own channels, and through our own ports in contradistinction to the trade that goes to and from the ports of a foreign country. The government might look up what other countries have been doing in this respect, because what others have done we may do

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I was very much interested in seeing the Minister of Public Works take the stand he has taken this afternoon in his purpose of opening up, not only the routes from the west to Montreal, but the routes from Montreal to the sea. I may say that in any scheme which has merits he will have my cordial endorsa-tion, so long as it is opening up Canadian routes to trade. I was a little surprised, however, at the proposition made by the hon. Minister of Public Works in relation to a canal twenty feet deep to North Bay.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Not a canal; simply improving the river.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I know, but the hon. minister will have to construct locks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The hon. minister gave no intimation that he purposed continuing that waterway to Montreal down the Ottawa river, but he gave the distance as 304 miles from Montreal to North Bay. It is eighty miles from North Bay to the Georgian Bay, it is ninety miles from that to the Spanish river, it is only 151 miles from the mouth of the Spanish river to North Bay, and at the mouth of the Spanish river on the north shore of the Georgian Bay there is a most excellent port at the present time. The Canadian Pacific Railway is in there to-day, and that being the case, why spend $3,000,000, or $4,000,000, in order to construct a twenty-foot waterway from the Georgian Bay up to North Bay when it would be of no use except for a few months in the year 1 If the hon. minister has a project to continue the canal up to Lake Nipissing, thence to Mattawa, then down the Ottawa to Montreal, if he can find a sufficient water supply, then, being in favour of canals myself, he will have my hearty endorsation. The Canadian Pacific Railway at present runs from Montreal to the mouth of the Spanish river on the route of the Sault Ste. Marie Railway, the distance being 515 miles. It would be an easy matter for these large ships from Chicago, Fort William and the west to bring grain from any of these ports, tranship it to the Canadian Pacific Railway at Spanish river and send it thence to Montreal. There is another matter that I wish to mention to the hon. minister. Navigators on the St. Lawrence claim that not only is the navigation of the

river very imperfect and very difficult, but that it can only be utilized between Quebec and Montreal during the day time, and that even below Quebec very great improvements are necessary in the way of buoying.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I can assure the hon. Minister of Public Works that anything in his scheme that proposes to develop the St. Lawrence route will have my hearty endorsation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Public Works, under the appropriations in 1900-1, asked for $433,000, and this year he asked for $419,000. By a reference to the Auditor General's Report of last year it would seem that the bulk of the expenditure of $433,000, authorized last year, or so much of it as was made was expended something after this form : At the town, or city, I do not know which, of Sorel, it would seem that the government had established large workshops, and that at these workshops there is in the employ of the government, and at day's labour, a perfect army of men. I do not believe it is in keeping with the principles of government that any one minister should spend such a large sum as $90,000 a year for day's labour in the construction of dredges and tugs and other Parts of the apparatus, because, I understood the hon. minister to say that some dredges were constructed at that place last year.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Is it a business deal on the part of any government to come down and ask parliament to vote moneys, and I presume he will appropriate this large amount, equally as much, to the same purpose in the coming year, upwards of $100,000, or more, for the construction of dredges, tugs or whatever he may desire. And. mark you, these are not to be constructed by public tender and contract, but the hon. minister is to go out among his party friends and ask them to send in their party friends and they are to construct these tugs. It is not fair to the city of Toronto, and I hope ray hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) will be heard from on that point, where they have shipbuilding yards that they are not to be given an opportunity of tendering for the construction of these dredges. Why should the minister have the right and the privilege and why should his colleagues assent to the proposition that he should have placed at his disposal upwards of $100,000 for the construction of dredges and other craft ? It is a preposterous proposition, and if we are to have dredges build for this country there should be the open principle of public tender, and instead of the minister taking $90,000 as he did last year, and I
presume he will take an equally large sum this year, or perhaps a larger sum to construct dredges, he should put the work up to public competition. It is startling that the hon. minister has such amounts of money as this at his disposal. Contrast this with other departments of the government, with the Department of Marine and Fisheries, for instance I know, that, in my riding, when that department wished to place out buoys, they openly called for tenders for the placing of these buoys. The work is ground down to the last cent. The competition is keen and the result is that this work is done at almost starvation prices. Take the Post Office Department; in Ontario, and I believe in the other provinces of the Dominion, there is the wholesome principle of tender, and tlie result is that people are carrying the mails at comparatively trilling prices. But, the hon. Minister of Public Works takes another ground altogether. He said last year :	I
want parliament to give me $400,000 with the right to spend $90,000 in constructing different kinds of craft, and it is fair to assume that he is going to take a larger amount this year for the same purpose. If he is not going to construct craft of the same kind, then, I presume, the amount should be cut lower, but, before the committee passes this item it will ask what the hon. minister proposes to do with this huge amount of $419,000. Is it in line with the policy of this government that they are going to assent to the proposition that the hon. Minister of Public Works is to have upwards of $100,000 to construct tugs, and dredges ? And, how is he going to construct them ? Is he going to ask for tenders and get the work done at the lowest figure ? Not at all; he is going down to Sorel, he is going to the representative of that riding, a party friend, and then all the friends of the government will be turned into this government shipyard to the exclusion of others, and the wholesale patronage is vested in the minister and the representative of that district. It is bad enough that upwards of $100,000 should be spent in this manner, but, we come to something worse than that, and it is the purchase of supplies. The committee will be startled when I tell them that the minister last year purchased, at Sorel, for the construction of these dredges, and other craft, no less than $235,000 worth of supplies without public tender. I would ask the hon. minister if that statement is correct ?

speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) should not forget
