maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: If the hon. minister says that these supplies were purchased by tender, no comment will be necessary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will make his speech and I will answer him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Were these $235,000 worth of supplies purchased by tender ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will simply finish his speech I will pledge myself to answer every point he makes now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Then, if the hon. minister wants to keep his supplies back he is going about it now in the proper way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It will not take long; I will answer the hon. gentleman in a few minutes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I simply ask the hon. minister whether these supplies were purchased by -tender or not. The hon. minister can answer that by saying ' yes,' or ' no.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I cannot now. I am just looking up the memorandum.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Well, I will sit down and let the hon. minister answer that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend should not forget what he has apparently forgotten, that he has only to go back to past history to remember that the shipyard in Sorel was established before we took office. I found it there, and I also found the same system of days labour in vogue. Indeed, that system is the only one that can be followed at Sorel. We have a shipyard in Sorel because we have a fleet of dredges, a fleet of barges, and a fleet of tugs, and so on. In case of an accident occurring, where could we go if we had not the shipyard ? The working of the whole system would be quite impossible without it. That shipyard has been in existence for many years, even when the harbour commissioners had charge of the ship channel, and in fact it is just as necessary for the government to have such a concern as it is for the Grand Trunk Railway or thei Canadian Pacific Railway to have shops. My hon. friend reproaches me severely for having built dredges by days' labour. Well, I take great pride for having done so, but I must pay the same compliment to the gentlemen who preceded me. I am sorry to say that I have just been informed that I cannot pay the same compliment to my predecessors, because they did not built dredges by days' labour although they built tugs and barges and so on. The1 best dredge they did build is the Laval, Mr. TARTE.
which was built at Hull, and without any attempt to discredit that dredge it is not the best of the. fleet. I claim that the dredges that have been built at Sorel by Canadian skilled labour are the best dredges that are in America. I do not see why the government should be reproached for building the dredges with Canadian labour in Canada. 1 would go further. I have often and often pressed my colleague the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) to have workshops of his own in this country. I claim there is no reason under the sun why the Canadian people should not do their own work in their own country. All the dredges which are working to-day in the maritime provinces are imported from England, but they are not quite as good as the dredges we build ourselves, and I want to know in God's name why should we import anything that we can build here. I may have faults

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I may have faults, but on that point I am a strong Canadian.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What about the furniture at the Paris exposition ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The furniture at the Paris exposition was bought before I went there, and when my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) goes to Paris and sees it he will agree with me that Canadian labour could have done just as well.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Then why did not the government do it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace) is quite capable of understanding the difference there is between building a dredge in Sorel and buying furniture in Paris.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I quite understand that the Minister of Public Works will preach protection in one place and practice the very opposite in another.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I feel there is a great difference between buying a hat in New York and building a dredge in Toronto.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: How does the cost of constructing dredges at Sorel compare with the price paid for dredges constructed in England ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The dredge that was brought from England cost a good deal more than the dredge we are building in Sorel.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The same capacity ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Yes. On that point I court the fullest investigation. and I would be very glad if some of the gentlemen on the other side

*would be good enough to come to Sorel and see the work that is being done there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Are we to understand that the dredges built at Sorel have cost less than dredges of the same capacity purchased in England ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The dredge St. Lawrence, which was imported from England, cost $115,000, I am informed. Her capacity is not half the capacity of our Sorel dredges, and the average cost of our Sorel dredges is $110,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: That is a saving of $40,000 in favour of building them at home ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I think they ought to be built at home then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I	think so too, and I may say that the dredge we are building in Toronto to-day will be built cheap compared with other dredges built elsewhere.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What is the price of the dredge which is being constructed by the Poisons in Toronto ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: For British Columbia ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: This suction dredge for the St. Lawrence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The cost will be $163,000, but of course there are additions that will have to be built later on ; there are discharge pipes and the like. This is an entirely new model and nothing of the kind has been built here before, and it will cost $163,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Did the minister ask for tenders for that dredge ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
No, I did not, and for the excellent reason that 1 thought it would be a waste of time. I was very anxious that the St. Lawrence channel should be dredged as quickly as it could be. I have seen at the Paris exposition models of suction dredges, but I was very anxious to build a dredge on American lines on this side of the ocean. I went to New York and to Bridgeport, where there was a large dredge that had worked in the port of New York for Messrs. Hughes & Co. I was received by the engineer in charge at Bridgeport, and I asked him if he ever came to Montreal, and he said : Yes, I studied at the Royal Military College at Kingston. It was a great pleasure indeed to meet a Canadian engineer in charge of such a large work in the United States. That gentleman's name was Morrison. There was another engineer by the name of Robertson, who is the consulting engineer for Hughes & Co. He is a Canadian who had worked for several years for the harbour commissioners at
Montreal, and since he crossed the line he has designed 116 American dredges. That man has made a plan for us. I learned since that he has also designed for the Poison Iron Works a small dredge that my department is building for British Columbia. We united Mr. Robertson and Mr. Morrison and the Poisons with the officers of my department, and we gave to the Poison Iron Works the hull and machinery of the dredge, keeping for our works in Sorel about $60,000 of the work. With regard to the supplies, we follow the same method as is followed by all the other departments. When we ask for nails or iron, we ask for quotations, as the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk, the Richelieu Co., and every other big firm in this country does, and we always get the goods at the lowest possible price. If my hon. friend would permit me, I would ask Mm to rise above party in matters of this kind. It would be simply impossible to ask for public tenders in such cases. We would be simply wasting three-quarters of our time without getting any better prices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The minister has stated exactly his position, and it is this, that on coming into power he found that there were some workshops at Sorel where repairs were made on government dredges. 1 quite agree with him that there was a necessity for such workshops. It would be absurd to argue that a government which had dredges and tugs should uot have a place to which recourse could be had for repairs. But the minister has gone outside of the question altogether. It is not of repairs that the complaint is made. It is because, on construction work, the minister, ipstead of calling for public tenders, gets the work done at Sorel, where there is an army of 450 men employed all the year round. Surely he does not say that all these men are kept employed to make repairs on dredges.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: We do not always keep that many there.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
The amount expended there, according to the Auditor General's Report, was $90,000. It is all clap-trap for the hon. gentleman to talk aborrt employing Canadians. Any person knows that wherever these dredges might be built in Canada, they would be built by Canadians. The hon. minister has stated his position, and I congratulate him, because he is getting stronger every year and does what he likes. He undertakes the construction work on this large craft, and the result is that he has in his hands this immense patronage, consisting in the employment of 450 men. All I can say is this, that it is well for the people of this country to understand the difference in the position of these ministers. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries may have a little contract ; that has to go to tender. The Postmaster General has a little

contract; that has to go to tender too. But, when the Minister of Public Works wants to spend $90,000 in labour, he snaps his fingers at contracts and tenders, and all such wholesome restrictions, and declares that he will do as he pleases, and spends hundreds of thousands of dollars among his party friends. Hon. gentlemen opposite were in opposition at one time, and if there was anything they ever did condemn, anil condemn wrongly-that is, the old guard from Ontario, who were here at one time, but none of whom are here to-day-it was this expenditure at Sorel. They condemned it day in and day out; but to-day nothing is heard from them, and the minister has carte blanche to spend what he likes. Coming to the expenditure for supplies, that is even more startling than the expenditure of $100,000 for labour. Would the House believe it ?-the minister last year went among his party friends at Sorel and distributed among them no less than $235,000 of public money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: On machinery, engines, and all sorts of things.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Let us have a look at some of these items. The minister says it was utterly impossible to have tenders called for these matters. All the other departments have to ask for tenders ; but the Minister of Public Works stands up and says that when he wants $25,000 worth of hardware, he cannot call for tenders for that. I find in the Auditor General's Report that a Mr. Cavanagh, of the city of Montreal, was given no less than $25,000 on account of hardware supplies. Does the minister mean to tell me that when he wants $25,000 worth of hardware supplies, he does not ask for tenders ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I mean that the goods purchased with that sum of money were purchased, I suppose, during twelve months, and after quotations were asked for every time.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Might I ask the minister if he asked for quotations from the leading hardware men in Toronto or any orner placi iu Ontario ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Yes, there has been a good deal bought in Ontario, and in Toronto.
ill'. CLARKE. We have in the city of Toronto some of the largest hardware firms in the Dominion. Did the hon. minister ask for tenders from those firms ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I cannot say that I asked for tenders everywhere, but I have often asked for tenders in Toronto.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Before I go into this matter of supplies, I -find that when hon. gentlemen opposite were condemning the Mr. BENNETT.
workshops at Sorel, there were only fifty men employed there, whereas the minister has now 450.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is a growing time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is, no doubt, and a growing time for the influence of the Minister of Public Works in the cabinet, on which I congratulate him. Now, let us take some of these items. First, Ahearn & Soper, for electric light business in connection with a tug, got nearly $3,000. Beauchemin & Co., of Sorel, got supplies to the tune of $2,253. Cameron & Co., of Ottawa, supply lumber to the tune of $8,292. The Canada Switch and Spring Company, of Montreal, received $4,407. Carrier, Laine & Co., of LSvis, received $4,955. Edward Cavanagh, of Montreal, received $25,000 ; B. J. Coghlin, of Montreal, $2,300 ; Dods Co., of Montreal, $859 ; the Dominion Foundry at Sorel, $2,239 ; the Dominion Wire Rope Company, of Montreal. $2,810 ; T. K. Foster & Co., of Ottawa, $974 ; the Gutta Percha and Rubber Company, $1,900 ; Kingman & Co., of Montreal, $20,000 ; the Laurie Engine Company, of Montreal, $5,584 ; E. II. Lemay, of Montreal, $10,333. I would like to ask the minister if Mr. Lemay, who* furnished $10,000 worth of timber, is not one of the harbour commissioners of Montreal, and one of the appointees of this government ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: He is one of the harbour commissioners, and a very able man. All those goods were got after quotations were submitted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I find the following firms down for supplies : Louis Bros., Montreal. $16,456 ; T. C. Moore & Co., $10,000 ; D. r! Macleod, Quebec, $15,600 ; McAvity & Sons, St. John, $2,000. It seems startling that the hon. gentleman had to go to St. John to purchase supplies for works at Sorel. Pate-naude & Co., Sorel, $4,422 ; Robertson & Co., Montreal, $5,297; Robillard & Co., $1,405 ; James Shepard, Sorel, $4,010 ; Wier & Co., Montreal, $9,510.
And so on. Here are thousands and tens of thousands of dollars expended, and the hon. minister gives us fair notice that after spending last year over $400,000 in the construction of dredges, tugs and so on, at Sorel, he is asking a similar grant this year, and it is only fair to assume that he will do as he did last year, namely, construct the tugs and what else he pleases without public competition. He and his friends who were opposed to our having fifty men there some years ago, are going to employ 450 men, and in addition to spend a quarter of a million dollars among their party friends. When we taunt him with not having invited competition, his only answer is that he bought at fair prices. Surely the wholesome principles ought to prevail in the construction of dredges and tugs of inviting

public tenders. Let me give one instance, in my personal knowledge, which will show the hon. gentleman's manner of conducting business in this matter of expenditure on tugs. His department had a very old tug at the town of Midland, which had been used there in connection with dredging work. It was necessary to construct a new hull because the old one was used up. The machinery of the old hull was taken out at the town of Midand and shipped to Sorel, where a new one was built, and the new tug was brought back to Midland. The hon. gentleman could have built a tug at Midland for the amount of freight he had to pay on the machinery, and the hon. gentleman knows it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: No, I do not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look up the accounts, he will find that the cost of transporting the machinery down to Sorel, and then bringing the tug back to Midland, would have built a tug at Midland, because it was not a tug of any considerable size. If that is the kind of .business method that characterizes his department in Sorel. the House should hesitate before giving him the opportunity of spending such a large sum as $400,000 in those workshops.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Our complaint in the province of Nova Seofia is that we have not sufficient dredges for the public works necessary to be done. We are quite prepared to build those dredges in that province, because, with the exception of the harbours of Yarmouth and St. John, in the province of New Brunswick, bucket dredges would not be suitable for our work. The kind we want in Nova Scotia, in the rough parts of our harbours and coasts, where there are a good many boulders on the bottom, is spoon dredges, and they can be built for $30,000 to $40,000 each. We would always have plenty of work for them. Some of those dredges have been built before in the province of Nova Scotia, and have done successful work, and I hope, therefore, that the Minister of Public Works will see that we have one or two dredges built in that province suitable for the wants. I congratulate the hon. gentleman on the influence he can exercise in this House, not only on the supporters of the government, but on hon. members opposite, and on the manner in which he looks after the requirements of the country, for whenever he finds anything important requires to be done for the improvement of trade, he is ready and willing to do it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: My hon. friend from East Simcoe is somewhat unfair.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am not attacking the hon. gentleman, but the principle on which he acts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: He has given as an instance an old tug in Midland. Well, that was out of shape, but the machinery in it was good, and we simply took down that machinery to Sorel and put it into a new hull. Where is the crime in that ? It was a business-like operation, which any ordinary firm would do. What I endeavour to do in the conduct of my department is what I would do in my own affairs, and what any ordinary business firm would do. I do not think that the business men of the country will share the views my hon. friend has expressed. The government is doing the right thing in building its dredges and tugs. My hon. friend says that that gives me patronage..

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Well, I reply that I wish I was delivered from patronage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Is it not a fundamental plank in the platform of the trades unions and labour organizations that the contract system on public work should be abolished, and the government do the work themselves ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Between that contention, which I know very well, and the other which my learned hon, friend advocates, I chose what I consider is the right policy. When I believe that a work can be better done by days' labour, I do not hesitate. And when I believe that it cannot be done as well by days' labour, I call for tenders. In this case. I believe, I am doing the right thing. In Sorel there are skilled labouring men who have been for fifty years building ships, and I am using the skill and ability of those men in building these dredges and tugs. If my hon. friend knew the people of Montreal better, he would find out that among those who have received patronage, there are some good friends of his. But I shall be very frank. I am a minister in this Liberal administration, and my duty is to give the patronage to my political friends, and my hon. friend, if he were in my place, would do the same thing. But what I do say is that when there is a manufacturer who does not share my political views, but who is the only or the best man who can supply me with what I want, then I buy from him. And when I find my own political friends who have the same article at as good a price, I deal with them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: But the hon. minister does not ask other people for prices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
I learned my trade with my hon. friends
/
1203	COMMONS	1204
on the other side, and I learned it fairly well. When I was oil the other side of the House, we used to protect our friends to the best of our ability. I am on this side of the House now, and I proceed upon the very same principle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that he considers it his duty to give this patronage to his political friends V

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: All things equal-yes. I challenge hon. gentlemen opposite to find that I have given one cent more to a political friend than the ordinary market price.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I see by page Y-34, of the Auditor General's Report, that the hon. minister purchased $25,029.17 worth of goods from the firm of Edward Cavanagh & Co., Montreal. Among the items is 514-9 gallons of boiled oil, at 87 cents per gallon. I ask the hon. minister if he will say that he has not paid one cent.too much there V I- am buying boiled oil for our company, and while it is higher now than it was between June 1. 1899, and June 1, 1900, it has not reached that price even yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: What price is it ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The price charged here is 87 cents. I leave it to any man who knows anything about the trade if that would not be an outrageous price, even at retail.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CONTRACT WITH THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) has found fault with us often about such matters-and as he is on the other side of the House it is right for him to do so, it is his duty. The other day he told us we paid too much for onions, and now he says we pay too much for oil. I have at the head of that department at Sorel an old officer, Mr. Howdon, who was fifteen years under the late administration. I have kept him there because he is one of the most honest men I have ever known, and he knows his work well. His instructions are to buy at the best market price. There are times, as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has suggested, when oil is higher than at others. But I should be surprised if Mr. Howdon, in whom I have implicit confidence, had paid too much iu this case. I thank the hon. gentleman for calling my attention to the matter, and I will look into it.

Manitoba-St. Andrews Rapids improvements, Red River	 $100,000
Explain please.
Is this item to apply to the St. Andrews locks contract ?

Yes. Last year there was a sum of $125,000 placed in the estimates. This year we ask for $100,000. That work has been urged for a number of years, and as I said, last year, parliament decided that the work should be constructed and a sum of money was placed in the estimates. The object of the work is to improve the Red river in such a way as to make it navigable from Lake Winnipeg to the city of Winnipeg. West Selkirk is the point where navigation now stops. From West Selkirk to AVinnipeg the distance is about twenty-three miles. Ten miles from AVinnipeg there is a succession of rapids. The object of the work is to erect a dam and a lock which will flood
these rapids so as to make that part of the river between AVest Selkirk and Winnipeg navigable for boats drawing seven feet. The work has been advertised and the lowest tender has been accepted, the contract going into the hands of Messrs. Kelly & Company for the sum of $469,000. This will not cover the whole cost of the work as the contract has been awarded only for the masonry. There will be a considerable sum of money required later on to build the upper part of the work. The work is composed of two parts-permanent masonry work 800 feet long, on which work there will be placed gates, movable walls, if I may call them that, which will be opened during the flood and which will be closed when the high waters of the flood are passed. When these gates are closed there will be seven feet of water at Winnipeg, the fall being about fifteen feet. Parliament pronounced last year on the principle of the work, and I am only carrying out the order of parliament in going on with it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. J. I. Tarte).

speechtext: Could the hon. minister say how much he expects the entire work will cost.

The estimate that has been placed in my hands puts the balance of the work at $200,000 in round numbers. It will be composed of a service bridge, movable frames, lock gates and working apparatus, lockmaster's house, shed, two steam travellers for loading freight, &c. Then, there is the ordinary cost of supervision, and, in round numbers, the work will cost $200,000 additional.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax.!. That will make altogether how much ?

About $660,000. If my hon. friend would like to have this little plan I shall send it over to him. It is simply proposed to flood the rapids that cannot be navigated now for a distance of twenty-three miles.
Between what points will this constitute a route, and what kind of traffic will go over it ? I am merely asking for information.

Of course my hon. friend knows that there is a large traffic in AVinnipeg. Fuel is very scarce in Winnipeg itself, and the object of this work is to create .navigation over the whole length of Lake Winnipeg and thence to the American frontier. The United States government have improved the Red river and made it navigable for over sixty miles. This will give access from the city of Winnipeg to Lake Winnipeg; in other words, all the district around , Lake Winnipeg will have water communication with Winnipeg, while, to-day, that water communication stops twenty-three miles from Winnipeg, which is a great inconvenience indeed.

The hon. minister will remember that tenders were called for this work a second time. The object of calling' for tenders a second time was to provide for a contract under the minimum wage resolution which was passed by this House last year. I would like to know if the minimum wage clause was included in the contract and whether that clause has been observed, whether any progress estimates have been paid, and if so, has the contractor hied affidavits to the effect that the minimum wage clause has been observed and such wages been paid.

I know very well that the work has to be carried on under the regulation respecting wages. No estimate has been paid yet. I have received from the Department of Labour a complaint that the contractors, Messrs, Kelly & Co., have not obeyed what is called the fair-wages clause. That complaint is before me. I am sorry to say that I received it only two or three days ago and have not yet had time to look into it. I intend to compel Mr. Kelly to follow those regulations, as he has bound himself to do. Every time that a complaint is brought to me I will certainly look into it carefully, and if I need the services of the Department of Labour, 1 shall be glad to avail myself of their services.
Could the minister tell us whether the figures in the second contract are the same as those in the first tender ?
I was not here when the tenders were called for, and I do not remember the figures. But I will be glad to give the information to my hon. friend.
What was the occasion of calling for tenders twice ?

Because the fair-wages clause had not been inserted in the first contract. There is a schedule attached to the contract which binds Kelly & Co. to pay wages up to a certain figure in virtue of that clause.
Transportation facilities-Port Colborne
harbour improvements	 $150,000

I explained this afternoon the nature of these works. I may say that a contract has been awarded for only 1,300 feet of the breakwater that we 'intend to erect. The whole length will be 5,700 feet. The Minister of Finance, in my absence two years ago, stated to the House that he thought the expenditure would not exceed $150,000. As the item passed through the House last year without any explanation being asked or given, we thought it only fair not to bind parliament to any expenditure of money larger than the amount already voted. But the contractors, Messrs. Hogan & McDonald, have undertaken to build the whole work for the sum of $395,000. As I have said, Mr. TARTE.
this breakwater is an essential and necessary work, without such we cannot do any trade at Port Colborne. At Buffalo, 20 miles from Port Colborne, which, as my bon. friend knows, is the entrance of the Canadian canal system, there are magnificent harbour works. The American government have spent large sums of money in building these works, which are not yet completed. The sweep of the wind on Lake Erie at certain times is as violent as on the Atlantic ocean. It is therefore out of the question to expect any large trade for the Welland canal unless we have harbour facilities at that point. The breakwater is the first work to be done. And I state here that I am going to ask from parliament the balance of the money-I do not require it this year, but I will ask for authority to build the whole breakwater. I would not stand in this parliament and say that 1,300 feet would be sufficient; there would remain a large gap of about 4,300 feet which, unless it was filled up, would make the harbour useless. Now, I wish to insist on this point, that Port Colborne is the first link in our system of canals between England and the west. That work is just as essential as the works in the port of Montreal, and without this improvement at Port Colborne we cannot expect any large freight carriers to come to our Canadian waters, it is out of the question. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals is performing the work that belongs to him, and I am performing the work that belongs to me. I hope that on this question we will have the support of both sides of the House.

I think it was two years ago, in the absence of the Minister of Public Works, a plan was laid on the Table of the House which projected an expenditure at Port Colborne of some $5,000,000. That plan embraced the building of piers and jetties, and an extensive amount of dredging. I do not think it included the construction of an elevator on any of the piers. Now, the minister has discussed at considerable length this afternoon, and more briefly this evening, the present position of Port Colborne ; and if any one bad heard him who was not aware of the circumstances, he would have been led to believe that never a bushel of grain or a vessel had passed Port Colborne. Now, what are the facts ? Port Colborne is on the Lake Erie entrance of the Welland canal. I think I am within the mark-and the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) can correct me if I am not-in saying that two or three years ago some 10 million bushels of grain passed through the Welland canal and passed Port Colborne on to Kingston and Prescott. Now, If 10 million bushels of grain went past Port Colborne through the Welland canal to Prescott and Kingston, it proves that this much-condemned place, Port Colborne, is not so bad as it has been described. Let me tell the Minister of Public Works that

for several years past vessels have gone through this entrance of Port Colborne carrying cargoes of 75,000 bushels of grain. Such vessels as the Rosemount, the Algonquin, the Rosedale, and others, have been seen from time to time in the harbour of Kingston, as the hon. member for Kingston will tell the House. Now, the minister has a proposition before the House to-night to expend $400,000. When this $400,000 is expended, he has partially completed a work which, according to the plans presented from his own department, will cost the sum of $5,000,000.
I want to ask the minister what will be the upshot of all this ? You can now carry from Fort William to Kingston a cargo of
75,000	bushels in vessels like the Rosedale and Algonquin as the hon. member (Mr. Britton) will tell you, and at Kingston that grain is placed in barges to go down the canal. As a result of this expenditure you will bring a vessel carrying one-quarter of a million bushels to Port Colborne, and you will transfer that to smaller carriers for Montreal. You will have to transfer that cargo to an elevator both at Kingston and Port Colborne if ever an elevator is built at the latter place. If you carry by large freighters to Port Colborne, you will practically close up Prescott and Kingston ; and I am informed that no grain went through Prescott this year, and a less quantity through Kingston. Can the minister tell the House what will he the saving in carrying wheat in large 200,000 bushel freighters to Port Colborne, as compared with carrying from Fort William to Kingston in 75,000 bushel boats. This difference in the cost of freight, If there be any, is the only benefit that will be derived from this expenditure. Surely the government had some data of this kind before entering on this large expenditure. I would also ask the minister what basin or area will be dredged to a depth of 23 feet at Port Colborne in consequence of this expenditure?

The point I make is this : Buffalo is 20 miles from Port Colborne, and last year over 200,000,000 bushels of grain and flour went through Buffalo, and it went there because the grain can be carried quickly and cheaply from Buffalo to New York. Between these two cities it is 450 miles by rail, and 500 miles by the Erie canal, which, however, carries a very small quantity of grain now.
I understand that.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman does, but this is one of the questions which the country needs to be educated upon, and the hon. gentleman may have something to learn as I had. If I am not mistaken it costs about three cents to carry a bushel of grain from
Buffalo to New York, and perhaps a little more at times.
Including the terminal charges.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes, Now, the cost of carrying a bushel of grain from the western points to Buffalo and to Port Colborne will be about the same. The point is how much will it cost from Port Colborne to Montreal ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Bennett) thinks that Kingston and Prescott will suffer. I hope they will not. I am confident tllat there will be trade for all the ports on the lakes, but the broad question is : whether the Welland canal will continue to carry only
10,000,000 bushels, as against 200,000,000 bushels received at Buffalo. It is not a patriotic policy for us to try and raise little differences between town and town. The main point is whether Canada will retain her own trade, and whether we can capture the American trade. Our route is the shortest, and the problem for us is to make it the best and cheapest. I feel confident that we will be able to carry grain from Port Colborne to Montreal inside of two cents a bushel, and if we can accomplish that, then when we have completed the port of Montreal and the deepening and the widening of the St. Lawrence, we are going to take the life out of Buffalo. We have only to put our hands and our heads together to do that. My' friend (Mr. Bennett) asks what accommodation we are going to have when these works are completed at Port Colborne. I believe the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) is providing for a harbour 1,200 by 000 feet.
What depth ?
Twenty-two feet.
At what cost ?
It will cost between $900,000 and $1,000,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: To make a harbour 1,200 feet by 600 feet, and 22 feet deep.

That is the entrance to the Welland. The entrance is to give a depth of channel of between 500 feet and 600 feet in width, and the excavation we will have to make will extend over a distance of about 1,200 feet. Our side wings will extend out, and we will have to dredge to a depth of 21 or 22 feet for the length and width specified. The work at the entrance is our work. In connection with one of the side wings, and as part of them we are making our structures substantial and sufficiently wide to admit (with one or

two projecting piers) of ships coming right straight from the lake and lying alongside the pier. There will be no turning and twisting to get into the pier, and there will be no difficulty in getting out. My hon. colleague (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is now asking for an appropriation for a breakwater which will inclose-for the purpose of extension and enlargement, if need be-a very considerable harbour, and it will he just as the needs arise, whether or not we will make a harbour of any larger area, and whether we will do in the future any rock dredging, of which -there will be a good deal. There is a large quantity of rock in that inclosure ; and whether we will dredge any of it in the future or not, we do not want to do any more than is absolutely necessary. My hon. friend (Mr. Tarte) was not present at the time the plan spoken of by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) was mentioned, and I think, produced ; and I would like to remind the House, as I think the hon. member himself recollects, that it was stated very distinctly at that time that it was a plan, covering the whole of the work which the engineer would advise us to do, and had not been passed upon by either the present minister or the acting minister, nor had it been considered by the government. It was the suggestion of the engineer of the department. It was a very expensive plan. He proposed dredging out the whole of this basin all the way from the breakwater to the canal piers, and providing for piers being thrown out inclosing the whole basin between the breakwater and the canal entrance. It would not be fair to treat that plan as a concluded policy on the part of the government, because it* had never been considered.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In other words, the engineer who made the surveys simply showed on -the plan what could be done if it should become necessary latei on. The plans which we are carrying out have nothing to do with that big plan, which I hope it may become necessary later on to carry out. If we were in a position to receive 100,000,000 Trashels of grain in a couple of years, or were capable of supplanting Buffalo, I am sure this parliament would not hesitate to spend a couple of millions to do so.
May I ask if the contract has been let for the work which the j minister alludes to, and, if so, who the contractors are ?
The contract has been let to 1 Messrs. Hogan & Macdonell.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The Minister of Public Works has not answered the question I asked him. Whip1 to-day you are carrving cargoes in vessels of 75,000 'bushels capacity Mr. BLAIR.
to Kingston, which cargoes you discharge into barges going down the canal, what would be the lessened cost when you fire to carry in larger vessels to Port Colborne, and transfer there to barges which will go to Montreal ? Has the department any data to show that ?

Nobody can have any exact data as to that; but experience has shown that waterways are the cheapest means of transportation. We have now a fourteen-foot channel between Port Colborne and Montreal, and by transhipping at Port Colborne into boats of fourteen feet draught, we shall necessarily decrease the cost of transportation from the west to the east. That seems to me just as clear as daylight. We shall certainly have enterprising people who will build fleets of large boats. I quite grant that we are short of Canadian bottoms. This is one of the difficulties, but all these matters will be settled in time. When the trade is there and the improvements are completed, the fleets will come. For the moment, what I consider important is to prepare the accommodation for the freight. The deep water channel would be nothing without harbour facilities. Port Colborne is in the same position as Buffalo, and there is no reason why, with a fourteen-foot channel, we could not carry trade more successfully through Canadian waters than the New York Central does to New York.

The minister has made the exact statement which I wished him to make. His statement is that despite the fact that millions of bushels of grain have gone through the Welland canal system to Kingston in barges of 75,000 bushels capacity, and that grain has been going to Montreal, he is now asking the country to pledge itself, and the country is going to do so, to an expense of nearly $1,500,000-to do what ? To try the experiment of transferring the grain at Port Colborne instead of at Kingston. If you had to take 10,000,000 or 100,000,000 bushels of grain to Montreal, you could do exactly as has been done in years past-take it to Kingston in 75,000 bushel barges, and transfer it there to barges of 30,000 or 40,000 or 50,000 bushels capacity. The hon. gentleman says that has not been successful. He says, I am convinced that we should make a new experiment at Port Colborne at an expenditure of $1,500,000, of having larger boats to carry the grain to Port Colborne, and having it there put into identically the same barges as in past years have carried it from Kingston to Montreal. And the minister makes the astounding statement that his government are going to spend this $1,500,000 when they do not know what difference there will be in the freight. Would any business man plunge into an expenditure of that kind without having any idea of the saving that

would be effected ? The only advantage in favour of Port Colborue will be tlie lessened freight that there may be in carrying grain from Fort William to Port Col-borne in 250,000 bushel bottoms against
75,000	bushel bottoms to Kingston. For this expenditure of $1,500,000, what are we to have ? We are to have a basin 400 yards in length and 200 yards in width.
No, that is not the basin ; that is the entrance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What will the basin be on the inside ?

I think the hon. member knows the situation there pretty well. We throw out from the mouth of our canal two projecting piers starting in the form of a funnel. From the side of one of these piers we throw out a couple of cross piers as it were out into the entrance, of sufficient length to enable us to safely receive and tie up the largest crafts that is likely to come down the lakes. They unload there. That is where the elevators will be. From these the grain will be loaded again into the barges which it is anticipated with every confidence will be the mode of carriage from Port Colborne down to Montreal. We have no basin in the sense the hon. gentleman would convey. We have an entrance and ships can get right in, and this breakwater is designed for the purpose of protecting that entrance from the extremely heavy storms which very often occur at that point.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When you get inside of these basins after you have done this dredging, what will be the depth of water on the inside ?

Twenty-two feet. The hon. gentleman has affirmed, over and over again, that every year the steamers employed as freighters on the lakes are increasing in size, and that these large steamers are absorbing the traffic of the lakes. Why do they ? Because it is cheaper to carry tonnage in these large steamers. Every year the number of small steamers is becoming less, and the number of large steamers greater. When large steamers come down in the neighbourhood of Port Colborne, they are compelled of necessity to pass the entrance of that canal and go to Buffalo. And they must continue to go to Buffalo until we make suitable provision for them at Port Colborne. That is as plain as any proposition that can be advanced. The ultimate result, when we will have equipped Port Colborne, will be that these vessels can ride into the entrance of that canal, lie there safely against the winds and the storms, unload their cargoes into the elevators, and we will have secured all this
freight for our canals, which we are now losing.
We did not act upon any mere conjecture, but took the opinions of every shipper that could be reached. We took the opinion of every one who is doing business on the Canadian route, and also the opinions of some of those who are doing business by the Buffalo route. I read in this House two years ago a number of these opinions, and all agreed that there is no hope for the future of the St. Lawrence canals unless we put ourselves in a position to handle the cargoes that come down by large steamers. Relying upon the best expert opinion we could obtain, we deliberately came to the conclusion that the only remedy was to put Port Colborne in such a shape that large steamers could be induced to go there.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was there not a difference of opinion between the government engineers as to whether Port Colborne or Port Maitland was the best ?

We took the opinions of various engineers as to which port was to be preferred. Our engineer was decidedly in favour of Port Colborne. Mr. Thompson had no doubt whatever upon the question. Mr. Keefer said that something had to be done either at Port Colborne or Port Maitland. He was in favour of Port Maitland, and I did the best I could, in view of these conflicting opinions. I had these two gentlemen together, I let them cross-examine one another and cross-examined them myself as well as I could, and applying the best judgment I could to the differences which existed between them, I came to the conclusion, In which I was supported by the concurrent judgment of the chief engineer, that Port Maitland was entirely out of the question. It was a number of miles away, and there were other disadvantages into which I need not now enter.
When the steamers get into Port Colborne, their cargoes will be transferred into . elevators, just as they are at Buffalo. At Buffalo they are transferred into elevators, and thence into cars, and this is done at very small charges. Why ? Because they have established an elevator system up to the highest degree of perfection, and there are fifty or sixty elevators at Buffalo. When these same steamers come to Port Colborne, they will have also to transfer their cargoes into elevators and thence into these large barges instead of into railway cars, and we propose to go right through -with these barges from Port Colborne to Montreal, just as the trains go right through from Buffalo to New York. Sly hon. friend says why do you not elevate at Port Colborne, and load into small barges and then elevate again at Kingston ? Or if you take the large barges at Port Colborne, why not load into them and then go to Kingston, and elevate again at Kingston,

and transfer into small barges and take these down to Montreal ? But, there would then he two elevating in the one route when you need only have one.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My contention is, that at present you take a 75,000 bushel barge to Kingston, and you transfer then to any barge that will go through to Montreal. You take your vessel to Kingston and transfer into an elevator, and then into a barge, and on to Montreal. We agree on that.
We do not agree as to the necessity of transferring at Kingston.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If you take a 75,000 bushel barge
If you do not propose to have your big steamers at Port Colborne, you do not propose to have any business.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) simply excludes from our Canadian waters all those large carriers which are the favoured carriers, and wants only small carriers. It is well known that the size of the ships on the lakes is increasing every year. But, he does not want them at Port Colborne, but wants them at Midland.
They are going there anyway.

I am just dredging to 22 feet at Midland. Why ? Because it is necessary to have deep water there for these large carriers. My hon. friend wants them at Midland, but not at Port Colborne. That is not very logical in my opinion. My hon. friend is all mixed up.
No.

I believe he is. There are two kinds of ships navigating the lakes to-day, ships of small size and ships of larger size-and growing larger every year. We want both kinds. The small ships will continue navigating our canals, but the larger ships will come to Port Colborne. Last year only ten miillion bushels of grain came by our route. I make this prophecy to the House-that when we have completed our equipment at Port Colborne and Montreal, the Welland canal will carry five times more grain than it does-I believe at least five times more. Large ships cannot go to Port Colborne today. Do we want those large ships ? My hon. friend says, no.
Nonsense.
I said nothing of the kind.

He says that practically. If there is no accommodation at Port Colborne the large vessels cannot go there. Is that a fact or is it not ? We know that there is no accommodation and that the large ships cannot go there. And, if the hon. gentleman says we are not to provide the accommodation, that is another way of saying that he does not want the ships to go there. Let us talk plainly. Without necessary accommodation at Port Colborne those vessels will continue to go to Buffalo.
You would need to rebuild the canal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, you would need to rebuild the canal at an expenditure of $5,000,000 or $10,000,000. It is simply an impossible proposition.
Nobody suggested it.
The hon. gentleman from East Simcoe says, if his language means anything at all, that the transhipping should be done at Kingston
The hon. member for East Simcoe will never be responsible for trying to make the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) understand plain English, I can assure him of that.

If I have not stated the proposition correctly, then I should much like to know what the proposition is. The hon. gentleman has been talking of transhipping at Kingston. He told us of vessels going through the Welland canal carrying 75.000 bushels of grain and said that these boats ! should go to Kingston, and the transhipping

should be done there Into smaller barges for Montreal. I think I am quoting him properly in that, and if I am not I should be glad to have him correct me. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that there are not half a dozen boats going through the Welland canal carrying 75,000 bushels of grain. There is a line in connection with the Vermont Central between Chicago and Ogdens-burg carrying 70,000 bushels, but there are not half a dozen carrying 75,000 bushels nor anything like it. The fact is that all the boats navigating the upper lakes with profit are boats drawing from 20 to 22 feet of water. These boats go to Buffalo. The proposition of the government is that the Buffalo harbour is exceedingly congested, and vesselinen are continually saying that they want a harbour at Port Colborne so that they can send their cargoes by that way, and so relieve the congestion at Buffalo. Building a breakwater at Port Colborne will make as good a harbour as there is on Lake Brie. The hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says he does not believe that a good harbour can be constructed at Port Colborne. Well, he has been there and ought to know the situation ; buit I will venture to say that there is no practical engineer in the country who will not admit that, when a breakwater is built at Port Colborne as is proposed by the Minister of Public Works, there will be one of the safest harbours of refuge there that is to be found on Lake Brie.
It will be a closed harbour.

And it will be a harbour with 22 feet of water; a harbour into which even the heaviest vessels on the upper lakes can come. They can then go right up to the piers at Port Colborne, transfer their cargoes into vessels drawing 14 feet which will pass through to Montreal. There is no question of doubt in my mind that that will be the route which will carry the grain of the North-west in a very few years hence. There is only one other point I would suggest to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and that is that he must put more money into his estimates to put the Welland canal into the condition it ought to be in. It is in no proper condition now, by reason of the curves in it and by reason of the bridges which were built under an antiquated plan. It will be necessary to spend in the neighbourhood of $200,000 to put the Welland canal into a proper condition by the time the breakwater and harbour improvements are made at Port Colborne.

While the plan of the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Public Works, if carried out, would seem to do away with the large business that is now done at Kingston-and, in so far as it will do that, certainly I, as representative 39
of Kingston, should oppose any such plan- yet, if I understand it aright from the argument that has been brought forward, all this business that iis to be done, by the transhipment from the very large vessels that will come to Port Colborne in the future is practically new business. It is said that we do not get that business now, and if we had the facilities we could get that business in the future. Now, so far as that may be done, if it does not cost too much, I certainly shall not oppose it. In this estimate is an amount for improving the harbour at Port Colborne. As I said last year, so I say again that irrespective of these very large vessels, a large share of the improvement in the harbour is necessary, both as to dredging and building a jetty or break-water. Let me tell you how the business is done at the present time. As the member for Simcoe says, a large amount of business has been profitably done for some yars. There are four vessels, at all events, carrying-grain from Duluth and Port Arthur direct to Kingston, the Rosedale, the Rosemount, the Algonquin and the Bannockburn. They carry cargoes, in round figures, of 80.000 bushels, if they are loaded up to their full capacity they carry 90,000.
They cannot go through the canal with that.

But they go to Port Colborne, drawing from 15 to 17 feet of water. They have to lighten at Port Colborne, and from there the grain is carried to Port Dalhousie by the Niagara Railway, where it is taken on these boats again and carried on to Kingston. I am sorry to say that it is carried at a very high rate over this railway, and I think one thing the government ought to do soon is to take over that railway. To that extent, I am in favour of the proposition that has been so often mentioned in the House, of government ownership of railways. This railway stands at Port Colborne as toll taker on the grain carried from the west to the east, they charge a toll of two cents a bushel. That means that it would pay these boats just about as well to come from Duluth with a cargo of 60,000 bushels as with a cargo of
80,000,	because they have to lighten to the extent of 20,000 bushels at Port Colborne, and they have to pay two cents a bushel for carrying that 20,000 bushels the distance from Port Colborne to Port Dalhousie. Therefore, they have to pay $400 for that
20,000	bushels. Now, they could go through on the 4-eent rate from Duluth and Port Arthur to Kingston, and be glad to get it, and probably will have to do so for a good deal less. They have got to pay two cents a bushel for this 20,000 bushels that they lighten. That means that for the 40,000 bushels of grain carried by the canal to Port Dalhousie, they only get as their share two cents a bushel on the whole route from Duluth or Port Arthur to Kingston. That

] 219

won't pay, as tilings are at present. So they might as well come down with a 60,000 bushel cargo, and for this reason. They cannot get a 60,000 bushel cargo as easy as they can get an 80,000 bushel cargo. Persons who have grain to carry want as much carried as possible, and therefore it is easier to get an 80,000 bushel cargo from these upper lake ports. Now, these vessels that I have mentioned, each take with them two consorts or lake barges. Each of these lake barges will carry in round figures 50,000 bushels, therefore, each of these boats with its consorts brings down a cargo of
180,000	bushels. The barges do not have to lighten, they can go through the canal drawing no more than 14 feet of water. It is only the steamship that has to lighten, after which she goes through the canal with her 60,000 bushels, takes her barges again at Port Dalhousie, and goes on down the lake. That has been a very profitable business to the railway for some years.
Do these barges that are towed by the steamer from Fort William to Kingston discharge at Kingston ?
Yes.
They do not draw more than 14 feet of water, do they ? Why are they not sent on down to Montreal ?

Because we want them to go back as soon as they can. The steamship is too big to go down the St. Lawrence, and through the canals profitably. The barges could go through the St. Lawrence canals, but as soon as they are empty, after the discharge of the cargo at Kingston, they go back with the steamer.
Is that because they are a part of the steamer's outfit ?
Yes.
What is the tonnage of these steamers ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I cannot tell the tonnage, but they have a carrying capacity of 80,000 bushels! At all events, while they may go down with safety, it is not economical to navigate the St. Lawrence with that class of steamers. They are expensive steamers, and they cannot go down with a full cargo. Of course they have got to be lightened so that they will draw less than 14 feet. If you have only 14 feet in the canal, you cannot load them for 14 feet, they cannot draw that. In order to have safe navigation, you have to have at least one foot of water under the keel of the boat.
You have got more than that in the canal, except in the locks.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: A boat will go through .a lock with three inches under her keel.
They have gone through with six inches.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That is the way, at all events, that grain has been carried. Now you propose to improve Port Colborne to accommodate larger vessels ; vessels that will carry a larger quantity of grain, than
80.000	bushels, as high as 250,000, then they will not have to stop at Kingston or Prescott to transfer, but go on straight down to Montreal. Now, two questions arise. One is what kind of vessels are you going to use ? You have either got to have barges, such as we have already, towed with steamships, else you will not have safe navigation of Lake Ontario, because, as the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Calvin) said this afternoon, Lake Ontario is a large lake and requires a very staunch and seaworthy vessel to carry grain safely. The scheme that is before us for improving the harbour at Port Colborne by deepening it, and by building this pier, is something that is needed, even for the present for bringing grain down. Of course it is very rough sometimes at Port Colborne. Even if there is 18 feet of water in the harbour, a vessel drawing 17 feet of water cannot go safely through in rough weather, everybody knows that. Therefore, it requires deepening, and it requires breakwater protection in order to give facilities for the present mode of carrying grain.
I do not want to commit myself, and I do not commit myself to any large scheme of building elevators at Port Colborne, but, generally, the transhipment of grain there for the purpose of the St. Lawrence route, the improvements that are necessary in the harbour and the consequent expenditure of money, are things that are urgently needed. I remember last year that the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) spoke about this Niagara Railway. I do not know whether he submitted it as a scheme or not, but what he did say seemed to me to be most reasonable and ought to have the consideration of the government. Just as much as the want of harbour facilities at Montreal stands in the way of the use of the St. Lawrence route, the Niagara Railway stands in the way of the shipping trade availing itself of the greatest advantages afforded by the Welland canal route. There ought to be something done to reduce the cost there. They are coining money with the quantity of grain that goes down at a two cent rate for such a short distance, elevating it at one end and spouting it out at the other. For this haul of twenty-one miles they get actually half of what the carriers get for bringing the grain down. This is something that ought not to be tolerated, and if nothing better can be done it would not be out of place, considering the large expenditure this country is making in providing transportation facilities, if the gov-

eminent bought out tlie Niagara road and used it as a link in the transportation system. Our boats have to pay, in addition to this two cents a bushel for lighterage, *canal dues of twenty cents a ton, and these are charges imposed on the carrier which reduce his profits to a minimum. This is something worth considering. I do not give it as originating with myself. 1 think the hon. member for Grenville is entitled to any credit for the suggestion which he made in regard to that railway. Now, I wish to say a word or two in reference to the fourteen foot channel. I read what the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals said in reference to that fourteen foot channel, and he blamed the transportation companies for rather throwing discredit upon the claim that there is a fourteen foot channel between Kingston and Montreal.
I did not say they all did that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not think it is in the interests of the transportation companies, nor have they any desire, to withhold credit from the government for doing what they have done, but I think they would not say anything in reference to the channel that is not borne out by the facts. There is a fourteen foot channel, but there are places where some money has to be expended to make the fourteen foot channel as it ought to be. It is not enough that there should be a fourteen foot channel just wide enough, or a little bit wider than is sufficient, to allow a vessel to go through. There must be a fourteen foot channel, and it must be so well defined that vessels can navigate it with safety and without the necessity of creeping along that part of the river. I did call attention when the estimates of the Department of Public Works were under consideration before to one point in the river and I will just mention it now. It is no part of the Canadian channel from west to east, but it is a place where you cross over from the Canadian channel to the American channel at the foot of what is known as Long island, the longest island in the St. Lawrence. The channel stretches above and below it, and it requires to be deepened in order to make it a fourteen foot channel. But, hon. gentlemen may say: why do you ask to have that place deepened so as to allow vessels to cross from the Canadian to the American channel. There are two reasons. American boats carrying grain from any American port bound down come up the Canadian channel until they get to that point, and if they want to lighter at Kingston they can do so, if they want to purchase supplies at a Canadian port they can do so, and then they can go over to their own channel and go on down, or, Canadian boats can use the American channel which is a straigliter channel between Kingston and half way to Brockville than 39*
the Canadian channel is. They are both good channels, but the American is the straighter and the deeper channel and Canadian boats use it. Now, I shall say a word in reference to Montreal. Enough has been said about that port so that I need not take up the time of the committee in stating what the port needs. What it needs now is that something should be done to relieve the carrier from the enormous charges made by the elevator men there. The elevator company are using floating elevators and charging half a cent a bushel for transferring grain at Montreal. They are coining money. I speak in the hearing of some shareholders of that elevator company.
Forty per cent.

They have made from forty to ninety per cent year after year. Something ought to be done to relieve the carrying trade from such enormous charges. Half a cent a bushel may not seem very much, but it is a good deal when rates are cut as fine as they are now in the carrying trade. If relief is given in that direction immediately before the harbour is equipped, it will be of great assistance to the carrying trade and we can at once begin to increase the traffic by way of the St. Lawrence route. These points suggest themselves to me, and I give them to the committee at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, in listening to the discussion here for the last two or three days of the transportation question and the best way of carrying grain to market, I observe that every hon. gentleman who speaks upon it has an object in speaking. He is speaking for his constituency and not keeping in mind the best way of carrying our grain to market. Now, if the government have devised a scheme, if after mature consideration they have concluded that Port Col-borne is the best point at which to tranship the grain en route to Montreal, if they have had the advice of the best engineers, I do not think it is right for us to stand and quibble about that amount in the estimates. I notice that the hon. member for East Siimcoe (Mr. Bennett) wants all the trade drawn to the port of Midland. He wants all the vessels to go to Midland, while the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) has a word to say for Kingston. We heard the other evening of the port of Halifax as being the place where the trade should go. and the hon. member for Welland Mr. German), of course, has been standing up for the system adopted by the government. We also heard from Toronto the other day. If the government have a well-devised scheme, and if it is shown that we can carry grain cheaper by adopting that scheme in preference to any other, for pity sake do

not let us quarrel about it. Let us pass the estimates and have done with it. I do not want to give the committee any plan because I think the plan which the government have presented is better than any plan which I could put forth, and therefore 1 cheerfully submit that the estimates should be passed and that we should get value for the money expended.

The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) said a short time ago that the distance from Buffalo to New York was 445 miles. I contend that our railroads from Port Colborne to Montreal are as good as the railroads from Buffalo to New York, and our waterway from Port Colborne to Montreal is better than the waterway from Buffalo to New York. Now, why is it that it costs more to handle the grain from Port Colborne to Montreal than it does from Buffalo to New York ?

One word more. If the people of Montreal are charging the farmers and the shippers of this country 90 per cent for the use of their elevators, I would not be a bit surprised if Portland were made the outport. The people of Montreal are inducing shippers to leave Montreal by that kind of exaction. I think the Montreal people ought to consider this matter well. I do not make the charge; I want to know if it is true.
I must admit that unfortunately it is true that there is a floating elevator company which has exacted very high rates.
I want you to see to it that they do not do it.

I denounced them from my place in this House two years ago. But that state of affairs will not last very long. When we have improved the port of Montreal, we shall have elevators. We have no accommodation in the port of Montreal ; but we are getting it now.
How ?
I have explained that over and over again ; we are building large piers.
You talk so much you do not explain.

I want to obtain a little information from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. I do not understand the works at Port Colborne very well. I gather from what the hon. gentleman said that the work which is projected there is a funnel-shaped enlargement of the mouth of the canal, and the side of it is about 1,200 feet long. Is that right ?
I have a sketch of it which I will show the hon. gentleman.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would like to ask one question of the hon. Minister of Public Works. I think he said that the present cost of carrying a bushel of grain from Buffalo to New York was about 3 cents, and he also said that after these improvements were completed the cost of carrying a bushel from Port Colborne to Montreal would be about 2 cents.
I hope less.

That would, of course, give that route a very decided advantage. What is the hon. minister's data for making that statement ? And perhaps he would tell us what is the present cost of carrying a bushel of grain from Port Colborne to Montreal, so that we may compare the two.
My data is that the' Parry Sound Railway is able to carry grain from Parry Sound to Montreal for 3 cents a bushel, and it is making money at that rate.
Does that mean carrying grain from Parry Harbour to Coteau Landing, putting it into barges there, and conveying it thence to Montreal ?

Yes. I have reason to know that. If the Parry Sound Railway could reach Montreal direct, without the necessity of transhipping at Coteau, I think we should be surprised at the low rate at which it could carry grain to Montreal.

Possibly there may be some more immediate connection between the charge of the Parry Sound Railway and the cost by this waterway, than I can at present see. The reason I ask this question is that it seems to be most important to know to what extent we can depend upon the opinion which the hon. gentleman gives to the House. I would also like to ask : does that include, as I understand, the 3-cent rate from Buffalo to New York includes, the terminal charges ?
Yes, it does.

I did not know that this discussion was coming on to-night, as I have some statements which I have gathered from reliable sources on the whole subject, and which I intend to have when my estimates come up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I may say that I am well informed that Mr. Booth carries grain from Duluth and other western points to Montreal for inside of 5 cents a bushel, and I believe it does not cost him more than 1 cent a bushel, or perhaps a trifle more, to carry it to Parry Sound. From Parry Sound to Montreal he

can carry for inside of 3 cents a bushel, and make a profit. He lias his own terminals at Parry Sound. He should have his own terminals at Montreal. When the government have equipped our canals, and when we have terminals, either our own or terminals which would be under our control, we would be very unfortunate indeed if we were not able to do what the private corporations can do.
The hon. minister did not answer my question, as to the present cost per bushel of carrying from Port Colborne to Montreal.

It is rather difficult to answer that question, because there is no rate quoted that I know of from Port *Colborne to Montreal. The rate from Kingston to Montreal is cents per bushel. Then you would have to apportion the rate from western points to Kingston, which is 4 cents.

Perhaps the hon. member for Kingston could give me the information I desire. I see the difficulty he suggests : the rate to Kingston and the rate from there to Montreal are through rates. Therefore, it is impossible to say, except on a mere estimate, what the rate is from Port Colborne to Montreal. Will the hon. member for Kingston be good enough to explain to me how the rate by the Parry Sound Railway, referred to by the hon. Minister of Public Works, compares with the rate by water through the Welland canal to Montreal ?

Of course we cannot tell, but we have understood that the rate by rail has been so cut that it is a little under what has been the ordinary rate by water, and that the railways have got business by cutting in that way. While I do not know the exact rate, it is a little under what it has been carried for from Port Arthur to Montreal.

If the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is correct in saying that grain would be carried for two cents from Port Colborne to Montreal, it does seem that we might have a possible solution of the difficulty surrounding this grain-carrying trade. If this rate of two cents includes the same charges as the three cent rate from Buffalo to New York, it must give a decided advantage to the Canadian route. Is that what the minister intends to suggest ?
Yes.
The minister has referred to the Parry Sound Railway, but I do not see the sufficiency of his grounds for stating that the rate from Port Colborne to Montreal would be no more than two cents.

The hon. gentleman from Kingston (Mr. Britton) has told us that the rate between Kingston and Montreal would be one cent and a half, and the rate from Port Colborne to Kingston would remain at one-half cent. I may add to that statement, that I have met a great number of American grain shippers as well as Montreal shippers, and their information tends to confirm that statement. The American capitalists who, two years ago, applied for a site in the port of Montreal, gave me valuable information as to the rates at which they could carry grain. Perhaps I may be told that they have not succeeded so far. Mr. Conners, I am sorry to say, has not got along as speedily as he expected, but the House must not forget that if he has not succeeded so far it is because the big monopolies in the United States could kill any individual who would try to fight against them. I know that several times he has succeeded in getting his money, and that every time they got at his men and simply took the life out of him. The information conveyed to me by the most important shippers in the United States was, that they expected to carry grain from Port Colborne to Montreal for two cents, or even less. I, of course, cannot give definite assurances. These rates vary, and when I speak of three cents between New York and Buffalo, that is the average rate, because in some months of the year the rate is higher and in some months lower. But, if by rail they can carry a bushel of grain between Buffalo and New York for three cents, then water transportation being admittedly cheaper, and Canada having a 14 foot canal system, it seems to me that when I estimate a rate of two cents I am making a pretty conservative estimate.

There are a few words I should like to say before this discussion ends. I agree with the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that we have the best all-water route ; in fact, the only all-water route ; but, there is a disadvantage which is to be found in the length of that route. Now, having spent such a vast sum upon our canal system in making it perfect, if there is a defect at any particular part of our water route, that defect ought to be remedied. There is a defect in the Lake Erie entrance to the Welland canal.
Hear, hear.

The Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and the Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) have declared that expert testimony has caused them to come to the conclusion that Port Colborne, rather than Port Maitland, is the best place to make good the defect in this water route. When the matter was under consideration on a previous occasion, I drew the

attention of tlie Minister of Railways to the fact that at least one of the experts appointed by his department favoured Port Maitland. 1 presume there is no use discussing that matter any further, because the minister, after the fullest consideration, no doubt, has come to the conclusion that Port Colborne is the proper place, and the government are carrying on tlie necessary works there to enable vessels of 20 or 22 feet draught to enter Port Colborne and discharge their cargoes there.
