The hon. member for Bast Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has pointed out a fact that cannot be controverted when he stated, that the only advantage that will result to our all-water route by the expenditure of this money is the advantage that will be gained by enabling vessels of a capacity of 250,000 bushels to bring cargoes from the head of Lake Superior to Port Colborne and discharge them there. That is the only advantage, after all, that will be gained, and whether that advantage will be sufficient to offset the disadvantages under which this allwater route labours, I am not prepared to say. The minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) tells us, however, that he hopes-I am sure we all hope that his expectations will be more than realized-that when the works at Port Colborne have been completed, and when large vessels are able to enter the new Port Colborne harbour, he will be able to reduce the rate per bushel for carrying grain from Port Colborne to Montreal to two cents, or a little less. Let me draw the attention of the committee to this fact: that according to the statement which the hon. minister has made, the Canada Atlantic Railway have been bringing grain from Parry Sound to Coteau Landing, a distance of 384 miles by rail, have been discharging it there into elevators, and again transferring it into barges, and bringing it 30 miles thence by water to Montreal, at three cents per bushel.
Less.

Less than three cents per bushel. The minister says that the distance by water from Port Colborne to Montreal is 375 miles, and if I took his figures down correctly, he said there was a distance of 384 miles between Parry Harbour and Coteau Landing.
And Montreal.
It is thirty miles to Montreal from Coteau, and, therefore, the distance from Parry Harbour to Coteau would be 354 miles.
Thirty-eight miles from Coteau.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
At all events, there is a land haul of about 350 miles, and there are two transhipments of grain between Mr. CLARKE
Parry Harbour and Montreal, and Mr. Booth has demonstrated the practicability of making a land haul about as long as the distance between Port Colborne and Montreal, transhipping his grain at Parry Harbour, and transhipping it again at Coteau Landing for Montreal, and doing all that at a cost of less than three cents a bushel. Now, in view of this, unless the minister can by these proposed improvements at Port Colborne materially reduce the cost of the carriage of grain to Montreal below two cents per bushel, it seems to me that his expectations cannot be realized from this large expenditure at Port Colborne. The minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) referred this afternoon to the proposition to expend a large sum of money to make North Bay one of the termini on the upper lakes for large steamers coming from the head of Lake Superior. He also spoke of the expenditure which is being made at Port Colborne. I feel very much disappointed that the hon. minister has apparently overlooked the manifold advantages that would accrue to the Canadian government if it had a second bow to its string by the construction, or part ownership, if you will, of a railway specially constructed for the carriage of grain between Collingwood and Toronto.
I did allude to it.

Unfortunately, I must have been absent. I think the hon. gentleman just alluded to it in passing, but it was a mere allusion. I do not think he held out any hope to us that a matter, with respect to which we thought he was so favourably impressed a year or two ago, would receive very much consideration from him at present.
1 want to draw attention to the fact that there is practically no difference in point of distance between Port Arthur and North Bay, Midland, Parry Harbour, Collingwood or Owen Sound. They are practically equidistant from Port Arthur. The distance from Port Arthur to Montreal by any of these routes is nearly 300 miles shorter than going round by Port Colborne and the Welland canal, and the most feasible route, it seems to me, that can be developed by the government is the route which will have Collingwood for its lower terminus on the upper lakes. The government are spending a large sum of money in deepening and improving the harbour of Collingwood.
Hear, hear.
They have promised, I think, to make a considerable expenditure for the purpose of deepening and improving the harbour at Toronto. I expected to have an affirmative nod from the hon. gentleman.
I will speak by-and-by.
I had hoped to have some sign of assent from the hon. gentleman.
You will have a friendly speech.

Both these works being accomplished, the distance from the head of Lake Superior to Montreal is reduced to 995 miles as against 1,296 by the all-water route via Port Colborne, thus shortening the distance by 300 miles, and of that distance of 995 miles less than 75 are by land. The entire distance, less about 70 miles, is by water.
I need not appeal to the committee that it would be a very great advantage indeed, as supplementing the water route, if the government would give favourable consideration to the proposition to acquire a controlling interest in the road specially to be constructed for the carriage of grain between Toronto and Collingwood. I do not know whether these large freighters that carry grain to Buffalo receive return cargoes or not.
Yes.
They take back coal.

But there would be a great deal more likelihood of vessels running to Collingwood from the head of Lake Superior obtaining return cargoes, if there was a route established from Collingwood to Toronto and from Toronto to Montreal or Quebec. The advantages are so obvious that I do not think I need take up the time of the committee in enumerating them. The hon. the Minister of Public Works has been to Toronto and has given some attention to the matter. He has discussed it with the members of the board of trade and he had the pleasure of listening yesterday to the hon. member for East .Toronto (Mr. Kemp), who pointed out some of the advantages that would obtain if more consideration were given to the establishment of Canadian marine on the upper lakes and the lower lakes as well. I am perfectly satisfied that if the hon. Minister of Public Works will spend one-half as much time in considering the advantages to be obtained by the people generally from the establishment of this almost direct route for the transport of grain to the seaboard, he will come down-if not in the next supplementary estimates, at the next session-and ask for a grant, not only to deepen the harbour at Toronto, but also for the construction of an air line between Collingwood and the Queen City. It is not unreasonable to ask him, in view of the representations made by both sides of the House and those of the board of trade of Toronto, not to overlook this matter longer, and not to forget the claims of Toronto harbour and the Collingwood and Toronto route. That route will be 300 miles shorter than the all-water route. If the government can afford to spend a million and a half or two millions on what has not passed beyond
the experimental stage, it is not unreasonable to ask them to make a moderate expenditure in the harbour of Toronto and on the construction of an air line. These works being completed, we will have the shortest, the most direct and best route from the head of Lake Superior to Montreal.

be much better spent on the Toronto and Collingwood route. There Is doubtless a certain justification for this government in spending money on the former route. They have this justification, at all events, that their predecessors spent such large sums upon that route that they must keep it in proper condition, and to that extent I am with the government, but they have advanced the further argument that they must put the harbour of Port Colborne in such a condition that it will compete with the harbour of Buffalo. Well, Sir, I have submitted to this parliament and I submit again, that the transhipment at Collingwood would be no more expensive than the transhipment at Port Colborne.
What is the mileage of that railway ?
It is eighty miles as it goes now, but sixty miles as the crow flies, and through a country easy for railway construction.
Watch the crow fly.

My hon. friend (Mr. Maxwell) says ' watch the crow.' Certainly there are a number of vultures, at any rate, when it comes to distributing public money through different parts of the country. I do not care for the jeers, if we get fair-play. The money should be spent on the best route, and the best route, if you take mileage into consideration, is via Collingwood and Toronto. There is every justification I believe for maintaining the Port Colborne route in its present efficiency; but to squander more money on Port Colborne I hold, is not justified by the information we have. I was going to say that transhipment at Port Colborne will cost no less than at Collingwood and at Port Dalhousie no less than at Toronto. The question Is : Is it cheaper to take a vessel through the Welland canal having regard to the delay necessarily involved in canal navigation, or is it cheaper to take a vessel load of grain down by rail I submit that it is cheaper to take the load by rail from Collingwood to Toronto than it is to take it through the Welland canal. In Collingwood, I am very glad to say, we have received fair consideration at the hands of the government. We have advanced in our work in a way satisfactory to the citizens of Collingwood, if we are to judge by the votes they have given in the last two elections. The question we are now discussing is not so much the vote at Collingwood as the general question which route should receive the consideration of this government. If you take the mileage there is no doubt about it, it is the shortest. And I submit that with an expenditure of a far less sum than would be necessary to improve Port Colborne harbour, the harbour of Collingwood would be made far better than Port Colborne, and you would then have a complete route, Mr. McCarthy.
not a waterway I admit, but the transhipment would be the same, and you would have a shorter route which would* be in the best interests of the country.

I think I cannot be accused of having overlooked the importance of the air line between Collingwood and Toronto. We are improving Collingwood harbour. The road is not yet built between Toronto and Collingwood. My hon. friend says he has expected a friendly nod from me in reference to Toronto harbour.
I have been expecting it for some days.

We have not treated Toronto too badly. We are carrying out large works of improvement there, but we are in the difficult position that at Toronto the two jetties that lead into the inside harbour have been built on a quicksand, and it will be difficult to give much additional depth without incurring a large expenditure. I do not accuse any engineer, especially those who are no more, of having been unwise, but all the same, it is a well known fact that all the harbours in Ontario have been built on a twelve-foot basis. We have to rebuild the whole thing, practically, because the conditions have changed. I fully recognize that the route indicated by my hon. friends would be the shortest route, but I beg of them not to deprecate any other route. There are forty millions of tons of freight originating in the great lakes. There is trade for all the ports. I claim that Georgian Bay is, perhaps, the greatest trade reservior in the world. Collingwood, Owen Sound, Midland, Parry Harbour-all the harbours of Georgian Bay should be equipped so as to receive the trade from the west. I think that if we give our best consideration to the different routes and the ways and means of getting freight for Canada, we might, in a few years, be surprised at the results we were able to achieve. I am always sorry when I hear a member of parliament deprecating any of the Canadian routes. All the roads that lead to the great St. Lawrence route are good. I was accused once of having made a speech in which I was for everybody. Well, I honestly believe that all the ports on Georgian Bay may be great recipients of trade; but I would like that every bushel of grain, every ton of freight carried to these ports should be carried further down to Canadian waters. That is a point we should never lose sight of, and that is the reason why, at times,
I feel a little sore about Midland. We are carrying on great works there, but a good deal of the trade which comes from Midland is taken to American ports. If some morning, I can find a way of stoppiug that and directing the trade to our own ports.
I will do it. I do not blame the Grand

Trunk Kailway, because we have not in Montreal harbour facilities that would justify us iu taking strong measures even if we were able to do so. But, when the St. Lawrence is equipped and the port of Montreal is equipped, I do not think that there will be any railway strong enough to take its stand against Canada.

I would like to ask the hon. minister when he expects to have the port of Montreal equipped. I have been listening to a good deal of discussion; and the minister perhaps, thought I was a little rough when 1 complained that there was more talk than explanation. I did not want to be offensive. But I think the hon. minister will allow me to say that I do not think it helps him to get his estimates through to be talking all the while, instead of giving explanations in a few words. I have no interest in one of these harbours more than in another. My only interest is to see that the money we vote in parliament is expended where it will be best in the interest of the whole country. I do not care whether it is Midland, Collingwood, Port Colborne, Parry Sound or any other port. When the whole case comes to be summed up, it seems to me that the Minister of Railways and Canals and the Minister of Public Works are competing with Mr. Booth and that it is Mr. Booth who is lowering the rates and not our canal system. Our canals are not carrying the grain to-day, as I understand it, as cheaply as Mr. Booth is carrying it by his railway to Montreal. What does that prove ? It proves that, after you get your great improvements at Port Colborne completed, after you complete your Welland canal, after you get your great equipment at Montreal, Mr. Booth is going to carry the grain.
Now, the Minister of Public Works says that it is because Port Colborne is not properly equipped that there is a falling off in the amount of grain carried through the Welland canal. I do not see it that way. It is because Mr. Booth is carrying grain cheaper than you can carry it by waterway, and he is carrying grain that formerly went through the Welland canal. The hon. gentleman shakes his head ; but will he tell me there is not as much grain carried to the seaboard now as there used to be ? Will the Minister of Public Works take the ground to-night that there are as many bushels of grain carried to the seaboard as formerly ? Either he must take that ground, or admit the fact that the Booth railway is carrying grain that used to go through the Welland canal.
Now. I do not understand the contention between the member for Simcoe on the one hand and the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Railways and Canals on the other. The Minister of Public Works is fighting for this principle, that if he can get
the amount of money spent at Port Colborne that he wishes, he is going to have a larger class of vessels, carrying 250,000 bushels, coming to Port Colborne that are now going to Buffalo. By doing so he thinks that he is going to reduce the rate of carrying that grain down to Montreal. Now, the member for Simcoe and the member for Kingston recall a fact to my mind that has uot been controverted. Men are bringing grain to-day from Lake Superior down with vessels carrying 80,000 bushels, and each vessel has two consorts carrying 50,000 each, or 180,000 bushels altogether. They are now bringing this grain to Port Colborne. But the difficulty is that an 80,000-busliel vessel cannot get through the locks, therefore, she has to be lightened at Port Colborne, and the grain taken off is carried by railway down to Port Dalhousie, and then taken on again. Now, is it not a fact that this class of vessels do not pay under these circumstances ? That fact has not been controverted by the member for Kingston. Grain has to be transhipped at Port Colborne and Port Dalhousie before it can be sent down to Montreal, that is a portion of it. How are you going to overcome that fact ? You have to have a better class of vessels to carry freight from Port Colborne to Kingston than a class that will pay to take it from Kingston to Montreal. There is the difficulty. If the hon. gentleman succeeds I shall be very glad of it, but I do not think, with the data we have at hand, he is going to effect the saving he expects. I do not think it is prudent to go on and spend the enormous sums of money that he has in view, because I do not think that prospects will justify the expenditure. I may say this to the Minister of Public Works. He is a younger man than I am, and if he takes care of his health and does not get too excited, he will live to see the grain of the great Northwest carried out by railway, and the canal system will only serve to keep the rates down to a proper level. That is what Mr. Booth is doing now. I am here to add my testimony of respect to Mr. Booth, for I believe his line is going to be one of the most important lines of railway in Canada for the transportation of grain from the North-west to the port of Montreal. Instead of spending so much money at Port Colborne, to my mind, it would be better to equip the harbour of Montreal so that you can handle the grain there, and not rob the people that are trying to get grain to the seaboard.

I would like to point out to the minister that the works that are being done at Toronto are works for the preservation of Toronto island. Those works are being carried on as the result of an agreement entered into years ago between the government and the city of Toronto. The government took the extraordinary position that before they would construct the

necessary works for (lie preservation of the island, which, of course, makes the harbour of Toronto, the municipality should be called upon to contribute a portion of the cost, and the municipality did contribute $100,000 towards the construction of the works that were necessary to maintain Toronto island. Now, the other work that we are asking the minister to provide for is a work that has been rendered necessary because of the action of the government. They acted, I presume, upon the advice of their responsible engineer. They thought the deviation of the course of the Don, which enters Toronto harbour, would help to cleanse the harbour of Toronto, and that it would remain as deep as it was before the deviation took place ; but instead of having that effect, the mud that is carried down in the spring and fall freshets has been deposited in the harbour, with the result that it is being continually made shallower.

Is not that largely caused by the straightening done by the municipality of what was formerly a circuitous river going slowly down to the bay, and not depositing its silt in the bay at all ? The municipality, I understand, straightened it and enabled it to flow straight down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Evidently the hon. gentleman cannot stand very high in the engineering profession, otherwise he would know that the widening and straightening of the channel rendered freshets an impossibility. There is no such a thing as a freshet in the Don since this great channel has been constructed ; but we have made a reservoir for the deposit of mud and silt that come down in the spring and fall, at a cost of half a million dollars. The municipality has provided a dumping ground for this silt in the new channel of the river. The point I want to make is this, that the city of Toronto is so reasonable in its request to the government that the government ought not to withstand the request any longer. The request of the city of Toronto is, that the damage to the harbour, which has been' partially filled up-the eastern part of it, practically, wholly filled up-as a result of the government works undertaken on the advice of the government engineers, should be undone by the government.
The hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) drew the attention of the House to the fact that Toronto is a greater distributing point actually than the city of Montreal ; and I am sure that the representatives of Toronto heartily sympathize with the Minister of Public Works in his desire to build up an all-Canadian route, and to secure as much trade as possible for our Canadian channels. I want to point out to the minister that if the harbour of Toronto is deepened to enable vessels of the full capacity of the St. Lawrence canals to come Mr. CLARKE.
in, there will be a stronger competitor secured for the producers and consumers of this country against the railways than by any other policy that can be adopted. If the Collingwood and Toronto route is established, as I am sure it must be, for it will continue to press itself upon the attention of the government, vessels drawing 14 feet of water can proceed from Toronto to Montreal and Quebec during the season of navigation, and they are more likely to get full return cargoes back again to Toronto than to any other possible point. Mr. Booth, in bringing grain from Duluth and Port Arthur down to Montreal, had to find return freights for his cars. Vessels coming to Port Col-borne, large freighters, that discharge their cargoes there, will have great difficulty in finding return cargoes to bring back to Port Arthur and Port William. But, with a line of vessels running from Toronto to Montreal or Quebec there is a greater probability of return cargoes being obtained through the entire season of navigation than by any other proposition which has been submitted. Now, I can point to the fact that the work being done in Toronto is done because of a contract made in good faith between the government and the city years ago. The work that we are asking to be done is to repair the damage which has been caused to the harbour of the city of Toronto, because of the action of the government and the government engineers in diverting the channel of the Don years ago. Surely this proposition is so reasonable that we may look for a substantial appropriation in the supplementary estimates of the hon. Minister of Public Works to have this work commenced and carried out to completion as speedily as possible. Estimates have been voted by the House before, but so far practically nothing has been done. May I appeal to the hon. minister that there shall be no further unnecessary delay ?

I may say, first, that I do not feel inclined to admit all the wrongs that the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says have been committed by the government. I will not place the question on that ground at all, because I think we might not agree. But, I will say of Toronto, what I have said of all the other points. If the air line between Collingwood and Toronto, after full investigation, is proved to be a practical line, if transhipping grain twice, once at Collingwood and again at Toronto, is not a barrier against that route, in spite of Toronto's failings, I would be very much inclined to do anything I could to help it, because, in questions like this with me here, there are no party politics. I hope that the House will share my views upon that. Montreal, Toronto-all points that can be made reservoirs of Canadian trade should be placed above party politics. But, I do not know that the hon. member for Toronto will rise in his

place and say that the question has been investigated fully as to whether the problem of the construction of 80 miles of railway. the transhipping at Collingwood and transhipping at Toronto, has been solved.

I will draw the attention of the hon. minister to the fact that it has been solved by Mr. Booth. He tranships from large freighters at Parry Harbour to cars, he carries the grain in cars down to Coteau Landing, he there transfers it from the cars into barges and sends it down to Montreal, and he does it for three cents a bushel. The difference in favour of the route which we advocate, as against Mr. Booth's route is, that, whereas there are 350 miles of haul by land that Mr. Booth has to perform and 30 by water, there is a haul of only 70 miles by land and of 300 miles by water by the Toronto-Collingwood route, and there are no more transhipments to be made.

But, the hon. gentleman must not lose sight of the fact that Mr. Booth's transhipment at Coteau Landing is only a temporary one. I may say that if Mr. Booth did not contemplate having a direct communication with Montreal perhaps he would not have tried to accumulate as much trade as he has done, but the Grand Trunk Railway were simply asking him to pay $150,000 a year to carry his grain to Montreal. He had to do something else and he has built an elevator at Coteau and is transhipping there. It is only a temporary arrangement, while transhipment twice will be a permanent feature of the air line. Speaking for myself, I would like, before we are too old, to have expert testimony as to the feasibility of that plan. The government are open to argument. If I were not a minister perhaps I would speak a little more freely, but, of course, if I were to say too much, I "would be accused of wanting to spend a large amount of money, I have notions of my own. I would like to see the trade of this country developed to the greatest possible extent before I die, and before I go to heaven with all the hon. members here. In other words, I would like if the country would do now what is to be done even if we have to spend some money. Some millions, more or less, do not amount to much provided they are spent with prudence, with care and with intelligence.

If the hon. minister passes to a better world before he has completed the reasonable works that we require at Toronto, and assisted in the construction of the Collingwood-Toronto route, I think he would regret it for all ages.

There are a few things that I cannot understand and one is this : The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) says that it is not the government's intention to either widen or deepen the canal between the entrance of Port Colborne and the other end of the canal because the cost of such work would amount to several millions. On the other hand, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Britton) says that boats arrive at Port Colborne with cargoes of 80,000 bushels that they have to lighten to 60,000 bushels in order to pass through the canal. The government say that their object is to bring in vessels bearing 250,000 bushels of grain to Port Colborne harbour, and in order to do that they have to build a breakwater at a cost of $(^950,000.
That is for the whole work, not the breakwater.
The total cost of the whole work is to be $5,000,000.
No, no.

I understood two years ago that the object of enlarging the canal was for the purpose of building elevators, enlarging the entrance of the canal, &c., and that this work would cost in the neighbourhood of $5,000,000.
Oh, no.

Very well; we will let that pass. The entrance of the canal is to be between 500 and 1,000 feet wide, 22 feet deep and 1,200 feet long. What is the object of expending this large sum of money at the entrance of Port Colborne harbour to bring in vessels carrying 250,000 bushels of grain, when it is now necessary to reduce cargoes from 80,000 to 60,000 bushels to enable vessels to pass through the canal ? If it is the case that we have to pay high rates for grain passing over the Port Colborne and Niagara Railway, if the company controls the rates, if the government cannot bring that company under control sufficiently to reduce the rates and increase the amount of grain coming into that harbour, what benefit will Canada gain by expending this large sum of money in order to bring larger cargoes into Port Colborne harbour without being able to put larger cargoes through the canal than are now able to pass through it ? Will the hon. minister explain that ?
I have explained that matter over and over again.
I will put it plainer.
Perhaps it would be better for the hon. minister to get his estimates passed and go to bed instead of going to heaven.

I understand the case, but I have answered at least a dozen times. The object of building the breakwater at Port Colborne is to-

allow the big ships that are carrying the, grain to Buffalo to come to our Canadian harbours and unload there as they do at Buffalo. There will be a fleet of steamers and barges of less capacity which will take that grain at Port Colborne down to Montreal. That is the object in two words.
That implies that these boats that come to Port Colborne are not to pass through the canals.
Some will and some will not.

But none will that exceed <30,000 bushels capacity. I have not heard any description as to what distance the breakwater is to be from these piers, and what distance these piers are to be extended into the lake. I know something of the harbours on Lake Erie, and I know the difficulties experienced in Lake Erie harbours at the present time. I know that at Port Stanley and Port Burwell, that there is a great difference in how you build the piers. If the arms extend in a funnel-shape as it is proposed here, and if the breakwater does not prevent the sand from washing in between these piers, you will be no better off than in the other harbours on Lake Erie. The western piers have to be extended a certain distance beyond the eastern piers in order to prevent the sand coming in.

I am not saying that there is, and I am not saying that there is not, but I do know that this is the difficulty in other harbours on Lake Erie, and that the government of Canada have expended thousands of dollars in dredging out the harbours because the breakwaters do not keep out the sand, and in view of that, very great care should be exercised at Port Colborne where there is so much money to be expended. I am not finding any fault with Port Colborne. Like my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane), I am willing that any harbour in Canada shall be improved if it is in the best interests of the country to do so. My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) said that this would make a great harbour of refuge. Well, in view of the large amount of money expended on it, it ought to make a fine harbour of refuge. Before sitting down I wish to compliment the Minister of Public Works for the interest he has taken in the harbours at Port Stanley and Port Burwell. We know that Lake Erie is a shallow lake, and that there is danger on it from storms, and I believe that a judicious expenditure of money now will place these harbours in such shape that vessels in distress within reasonable distance of them will be able to find refuge.

I wish to refer to a question which was asked me earlier in the discussion by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden). I spoke from memory, and after he asked me the question I telephoned to the general manager of the transportation company, and his reply to me is that they carried grain from Kingston to Montreal last year for If cents, which, of course, includes the elevator charges at Kingston. He said that if he was asked to make a rate from Port Colborne to Montreal, although there is no such rate made at present, it would probably be 2f cents ; perhaps 2i cents.
Perhaps less.
Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Britton) say that that includes the transferring charges at Kingston.
Yes.
Does it include any of the elevating charges at Montreal ?
I think not.
These charges will disappear in Montreal.
I thank the hon. gentleman (Mr. Britton) for the information.
We will take up the votes for public buildings, as there are no controversial items, they being all old votes.
There are some controversial items ; there are votes for immigration buildings at St. John and Halifax and Quebec, which will require some explanation.
All these items will come up in the supplementa'ries.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I know that, but we must have the information when they are being passed by the House.
We have been going on with about thirty members in the House for the last three hours, and perhaps it would not be expedient to go further.

It is only to make progress.
Halifax, new public building	 $25,000

I wish to ask for some information in regard to this vote. The site for this building was purchased some time ago, and there is urgent need for immediately extending the accommodation required by the Dominion offices at Halifax. The item of $25,000 would not be nearly enough for the purpose of erecting such a building. I would like to learn

from the minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) what is the cause of the delay in connection with the erection of the building, and if it is the policy of the government to erect it, why is it that we have not a vote which would be sufficient to make substantial progress, and if possible, complete it during the ensuing year.

I am just asking parliament to place at my disposal the sum of $50,000 ; this sum of $25,000 was voted at last session of parliament. We had a great many buildings to erect all over the country. We were just completing in Halifax a large drill hall. Perhaps we have not gone as fast as some of our friends expected us to go, but my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) may rest assured that no time will be lost now. I think I speak the views- of my colleagues when I say that the government intends to erect in Halifax a building worthy of that capital. We consider that Halifax is one of the most important cities in Canada. It is a kind of Imperial city. Without spending too much money, I hope that the new building will be a credit to Canada and to the city of Halifax. I understand that the plans are now completed.

There has been a great deal of delay already. I remember last spring arguing an appeal to the Exchequer Court from a decision with respect to the expropriation for the site which had taken place a great many months before.

It was not expropriated ; It was purchased. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) is referring to some other property. The city market building was not expropriated. I know it was purchased, because I negotiated the purchase for my hon. friend (Mr. Tarte.)

The term ' expropriation ' is, perhaps, not technically correct, but there was a question of the interest of one of the parties. The money was paid into the Exchequer Court, and it was practically dealt with by the Exchequer Court in the same way as if it had been expropriated. However, that is immaterial. The question is : what is the date when the site was acquired, what is the cause of the delay which has since taken place, and what delay will there be before the building is constructed ? It is very nice to know that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) regards the city in so favourable a light as an Imperial city, and so forth, but still that does not help us so much with respect to the advancement of this building.
I can only say that no time will be lost. I do not want to plead illness, but my hon. friend knows that I have been away from this country through illness. No time will be lost now.
I would not press my hon. friend in that aspect of the matter of that kind, but I would suppose that this would be dealt with by the engineers and the permanent officers of his department.
Well, no time will be lost now.
What is this building intended for ? Those of us who are not acquainted with the city of Halifax do not know much about it.

The building is intended chiefly for a customhouse, and also for other offices. There has been no public building for that purpose erected in Halifax since confederation. The public offices, so far as it is possible to accommodate them, are in a building erected before confederation, and with the growth of business it has been necessary to hire offices in different parts of the city. For example, the Assistant Receiver General's office is a hired appartment in one part of the city, and there are various offices connected with the customs and inland revenue scattered over the city. The object of this vote is to provide for these in one building. The present building is chiefly used for customs and post office, and both these departments need better accommodation.
What will be the probable cost ?

I think I stated, on a previous occasion, that if the building cost over $150,000 we would again communicate to the House. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has told me since, that he feels that a building of a proper character for the city could not be erected for less than $200,000, and that is one of the reasons why I have not felt like pressing my hon. friend to award the contract, because I had given assurances that in case It cost more than $150,000, the matter would be mentioned again in parliament. Up to the present time no contract has been awarded.
This is a small vote for a building of that kind.
The building will occupy some time in erecting.
Does the $200,000 include the site ?

The site was paid for by a special vote of $25,000. I fancy this will not include the site.
St. John Immigration building	 $11,000
This is to complete the building.

I wish the minister to explain what kind of building is in St. John now, what great necessity there is for this new building, and what it is to cost. I do not

want to enter into a general discussion of our immigration policy, but I feel that we are spending a great deal more money in that direction, and this vote will be charged to another account than Immigration.

I may say that we have no accommodation whatever at that port now. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) knows, St. John is one of the winter ports of Canada, and it is out of the question to try and bring immigrants there unless we have accommodation. The cost of the building will range between $25,000 and $30,000, and it will have to be equipped as a good immigration building should be equipped.
Was there anything spent out of the vote last year ?
No.

It is wonderful how you got along so many years without an immigration building there. I find from the returns that the number of immigrants landing at St. John is not very large. The people who travel to St. John are usually tourists and such.
All the same, if we are going to have a fast line, as I hope we will have, we must have an immigration building there surely.
Is it the intention of the government to have large immigration buildings at all the ports ?
Not all the ports.
Is there not one in Halifax V
We have one in Halifax and one in Quebec.
You are building one in St. John, and have you not one in Montreal ?
We have none in Montreal.
It is strange you should want one in St. John and none in Montreal.

The people of Montreal are very moderate in their demands, and they have taken care of their immigrants up to the present.
Buckingham building	 $7,000
Drummondville public building	 9,000
What did these public public buildings cost ?

The one at Drummondville will cost just $14,000, with furniture and everything complete ; and the Buckingham building will cost $15,000, with furinture. They will just cost what is in the estimates for them.
Some resolutions reported.
On motion of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, House adjourned at 10.50 p.m.
Monday, March 11, 1901.
